Conformal Individual Treatment Effect Estimation under Networked Interference

 

Matteo Zecchin†    Osvaldo Simeone§

†Communication Systems Department, EURECOM, Sophia Antipolis, France §Institute for Intelligent Networked Systems (INSI), Northeastern University London, London, UK zecchin@eurecom.fr, o.simeone@{nulondon.ac.uk, northeastern.edu}

††footnotetext: The work of O. Simeone was supported by an Open Fellowship of the EPSRC (EP/W024101/1), by the EPSRC (EP/X011852/1) and by the ERC (No. 101198347).
Abstract

Conformal counterfactual prediction constructs prediction sets with finite-sample coverage guarantees for counterfactual outcomes and individual treatment effects under the no-interference assumption. In this work, we relax this assumption by allowing each unit’s potential outcomes to depend on other units’ treatments and covariates. In this setting, propensity-score reweighting does not restore weighted exchangeability, and existing methods may fail to achieve valid coverage. To address this issue, we develop interference-adjusted weighted conformal prediction that accounts for interference by constructing an observable upper bound on the ideal and unobserved conformal pp-value under the target intervention. The resulting prediction sets provide finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees for counterfactual outcomes and individual treatment effects in both transductive and inductive settings. We also derive a sharper construction when intervention-induced changes in nonconformity scores are bounded. Numerical experiments show that our methods preserve nominal coverage, whereas existing methods may not.

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

Many practical decisions require predicting how a particular unit would have responded to an action it did not receive. A physician may wish to assess what a patient’s outcome would have been under an alternative treatment (Zhao et al., 2012), an online platform may need to evaluate how a user would have responded to an advertising campaign (Gordon et al., 2019), and a network operator may need to assess what would have happened had resources been allocated to a specific user (Bao et al., 2017; Hou et al., 2025). Such decisions require comparing the observed factual outcome under the assigned treatment with the counterfactual outcome that would have been observed under an alternative treatment. The fundamental challenge is that only the factual outcome is observed, while the remaining potential outcomes must be predicted from data (Rubin, 1974; Rubin, 2005).

The reliability of the resulting decision hinges on faithfully quantifying the uncertainty associated with the counterfactual prediction. Conformal prediction has emerged as a powerful framework for this purpose, providing model-agnostic prediction sets with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees for missing potential outcomes and individual treatment effects (Shafer and Vovk, 2008). Under the assumption that the treatment assigned to a given unit does not affect the outcomes of other units, counterfactual prediction can be formulated as a prediction problem under covariate shift, and weighted conformal prediction (WCP) (Tibshirani et al., 2019) can be used to construct valid prediction sets via propensity-score weighting (Lei and Candès, 2021).

In many applications, however, a unit’s outcome depends not only on its own treatment but also on the treatments assigned to other units (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Aronow and Samii, 2017; Forastiere et al., 2021). Vaccinating one person can change the infection risk faced by others; showing an advertisement to one user can influence the behavior of their peers; and allocating resources to one user can reduce the resources available to others. In these settings, intervening on the treatment of a target unit can alter the distribution of outcomes of other units. This distributional shift cannot be expressed via unit-level propensity weights and, as a result, WCP may fail to provide valid coverage under interference.

This phenomenon is illustrated in Figure 1. The example considers a simple model of local interactions in which each of NN units is connected to its kk nearest neighbors in covariate space. Treatments are assigned independently according to the units’ covariates, and each unit’s outcome depends on the fraction of its treated neighbors. When k=0k=0, there is no interference, and WCP attains the target coverage. As the number of neighbors kk increases, an intervention on the target unit alters the exposures of a growing number of units. Consequently, the discrepancy between the observational and interventional distributions increases, and WCP exhibits increasingly severe undercoverage.

To address this problem, we develop a counterfactual conformal procedure that preserves marginal coverage under networked interference. The proposed interference-adjusted WCP (IA-WCP) is based on a corrected pp-value computed from the observed data (Vovk et al., 2005; Shafer and Vovk, 2008) and knowledge of the interference structure. As shown in Figure 1, IA-WCP reduces to WCP in the absence of interference and, unlike WCP, maintains coverage as interference increases, at the cost of wider prediction sets. We develop IA-WCP for both transductive and inductive settings (Clarkson, 2023; H. Zargarbashi et al., 2023; H. Zargarbashi and Bojchevski, 2024) and establish finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees in each case. We also provide an example showing that the correction can be tight with respect to marginal coverage and introduce a sharper variant, interference-adjusted WCP+ (IA-WCP+), for settings in which intervention-induced changes in the affected nonconformity scores are bounded.

1.2 Related Work

WCP provides prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes and individual treatment effects under covariate shift and no interference (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Lei and Candès, 2021). Recent extensions of WCP address hidden confounding and poor overlap while retaining the no-interference assumption (Jin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Farzaneh et al., 2025; Qchohi et al., 2026). Separately, research on causal inference under interference introduced the notion of exposure mappings to identify and estimate direct and spillover effects (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Aronow and Samii, 2017; Forastiere et al., 2021). Conformal methods for networked data have primarily targeted factual node labels or links (Clarkson, 2023; Huang et al., 2023a; Zhao et al., 2024). The closely related method of Zhou et al. (2025) constructs conformal prediction sets for ITEs on networked data but assumes no interference. Our work connects these lines of research by constructing prediction sets with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees for individual potential outcomes and treatment effects under network interference. A more detailed discussion is provided in Appendix A.

1.3 Contributions

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate conformal inference for ITEs and treatment effects under interference in both the transductive setting, where the targets are units in the observed population, and the inductive setting, where the goal is to generalize to new units.

  • •

    We develop IA-WCP, an interference-adjusted counterfactual conformal procedure that produces prediction sets for the potential outcomes with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under interference, and reduces to WCP (Lei and Candès, 2021) in the absence of interference.

  • •

    Under a score-stability condition, we present a sharper version of IA-WCP, referred to as IA-WCP+, that can produce smaller prediction sets while maintaining coverage.

  • •

    We provide experimental results showing that WCP can undercover under interference, whereas the proposed IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ preserve marginal coverage.

2 Setting

We consider a population of NN units indexed by i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}. Each unit has covariates Xi∈𝒳X_{i}\in\mathcal{X} and receives a binary treatment Ti∈{0,1}T_{i}\in\{0,1\}. We write X1:N=(X1,…,XN)X_{1:N}=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}) and T1:N=(T1,…,TN)T_{1:N}=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{N}), and use X−i1:NX^{-i}_{1:N} and T−i1:NT^{-i}_{1:N} for the corresponding vectors with unit ii removed. The covariates are independently sampled from a common population distribution PXP_{X}, and, as detailed next, treatments are conditionally independent under a common covariate-dependent policy.

Assumption 1 (Treatment assignment and overlap).

There exists a propensity score function π:𝒳→(0,1)\pi:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1) such that, conditionally on covariates X1:NX_{1:N}, the assigned treatments are independent and distributed as

Ti∣X1:N∼Bernoulli(π(Xi)),i=1,…,N.\displaystyle T_{i}\mid X_{1:N}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi(X_{i})),\quad i=1,\dots,N. (1)

Moreover, there exists a strictly positive constant π¯∈(0,1/2]\underline{\pi}\in(0,1/2] such that

π¯≤π⁡(x)≤1−π¯,∀x∈𝒳.\displaystyle\underline{\pi}\leq\pi(x)\leq 1-\underline{\pi},\qquad\forall x\in\mathcal{X}. (2)

For a given treatment vector T1:NT_{1:N}, define the control and treated index sets, respectively, as

ℐ0={j∈{1,…,N}:Tj=0},\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{0}=\{j\in\{1,\dots,N\}:T_{j}=0\}, (3)

and

ℐ1={j∈{1,…,N}:Tj=1}.\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{1}=\{j\in\{1,\dots,N\}:T_{j}=1\}. (4)

For each unit ii, let (Yi​(0),Yi​(1))(Y_{i}(0),Y_{i}(1)) denote its potential outcomes under treatment Ti=0T_{i}=0 and Ti=1T_{i}=1. Departing from the standard SUTVA, we allow these outcomes to depend on covariates and treatments of a subset of units, excluding unit ii (Tchetgen and VanderWeele, 2012; Hudgens and Halloran, 2008). Specifically, for each unit ii, we summarize this inter-unit dependence through an exposure variable Ei∈ℰE_{i}\in\mathcal{E} (Aronow and Samii, 2017) that depends on units in a neighborhood set

𝒩i(X1:N)⊆{1,…,N}∖{i}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\}. (5)

The neighborhood 𝒩i(X1:N)\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N}) generally depends on the covariates X1:NX_{1:N}. For example, in Figure 1 the set 𝒩i(X1:N)\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N}) corresponds to the kk nearest neighbors to unit ii. Furthermore, the neighborhood relation may be directed, meaning that j∈𝒩i(X1:N)j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N}) need not imply i∈𝒩j(X1:N)i\in\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N}). Overall, the neighborhood relations {𝒩i(X1:N)}i=1N\{\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})\}^{N}_{i=1} define a covariate-dependent exposure (directed) graph 𝒢(X1:N)\mathcal{G}(X_{1:N}) with nodes given by the units {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\} and edges (i,j)(i,j) with j∈𝒩i(X1:N)j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N}).

In this work, we restrict attention to permutation-equivariant neighborhood rules. For a permutation σ\sigma of the set {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}, write

Tσ⁡(1:N)=(Tσ⁡(1),…,Tσ⁡(N)),\displaystyle T_{\sigma(1:N)}=(T_{\sigma(1)},\dots,T_{\sigma(N)}), (6)

and

Xσ⁡(1:N)=(Xσ⁡(1),…,Xσ⁡(N)).\displaystyle\quad X_{\sigma(1:N)}=(X_{\sigma(1)},\dots,X_{\sigma(N)}). (7)
Assumption 2 (Permutation-equivariant neighborhood rule).

For any permutation σ\sigma of the set {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}, and every unit i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\dots,N\}, the neighborhood rule satisfies

𝒩i(Xσ⁡(1:N))={j:σ(j)∈𝒩σ⁡(i)(X1:N)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)})=\left\{j:\sigma(j)\in\mathcal{N}_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N})\right\}. (8)
Example:

Given a distance d:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} and a radius r≥0r\geq 0, the radius-rr neighborhood rule corresponds to 𝒩i(X1:N)={j≠i:d(Xi,Xj)≤r}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\left\{j\neq i:d(X_{i},X_{j})\leq r\right\}.

This rule satisfies Assumption 2 since permutations of units preserve pairwise distances. For illustration, consider X1=0X_{1}=0, X2=0.5X_{2}=0.5, and X3=1X_{3}=1, with d⁡(x,x′)=|x−x′|d(x,x^{\prime})=|x-x^{\prime}|, r=0.6r=0.6, and a permutation σ⁡(1)=2,σ⁡(2)=3,σ⁡(3)=1\sigma(1)=2,\sigma(2)=3,\sigma(3)=1.

Then, we have Xσ⁡(1:3)=(X2,X3,X1)X_{\sigma(1:3)}=(X_{2},X_{3},X_{1}) and, for i=1i=1, the neighborhood set is 𝒩1(Xσ⁡(1:3))={j≠1:d(Xσ⁡(1),Xσ⁡(j))≤0.6}={2,3}\mathcal{N}_{1}(X_{\sigma(1:3)})=\left\{j\neq 1:d(X_{\sigma(1)},X_{\sigma(j)})\leq 0.6\right\}=\{2,3\}, which can be seen to satisfy Assumption 2. More examples of neighborhood rules satisfying this property are given in Appendix B.

We define the multiset of treatments and covariates for units in neighborhood 𝒩i(X1:N)\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N}) as

ℒi(X1:N,T1:N)={{(Xj,Tj):j∈𝒩i(X1:N)}},\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})=\bigl\{\bigl\{(X_{j},T_{j}):j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})\bigr\}\bigr\}, (9)

where the doubled braces indicate that repeated covariate–treatment pairs are retained with their multiplicities. Each exposure variable EiE_{i} depends only on XiX_{i} and variables in the multiset ℒi(X1:N,T1:N)\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}) as detailed next.

Assumption 3 (Exposure generation and observation).

Conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}), the exposure variables E1,…,ENE_{1},\dots,E_{N} are independent. Moreover, there exists a common conditional distribution PE|X,ℒP_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}} such that, for each i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, we have

Ei∣(X1:N,T1:N)∼PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xi,ℒi(X1:N,T1:N)).\displaystyle E_{i}\mid(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{i},\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right). (10)

Each exposure EiE_{i} is either directly observed or can be exactly recovered from XiX_{i} and the multiset ℒi(X1:N,T1:N)\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}).

The assumption that the exposure variable EiE_{i} is observable is natural when the exposure mechanism is known. Examples include the number or fraction of treated neighbors within a known group or cluster and distance-weighted exposures that depend on observed covariates (Aronow and Samii, 2017; Forastiere et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2024).

Assumption 4 (No hidden interference confounding).

Conditional on the covariates, exposures, and treatments (X1:N,E1:N,T1:N)(X_{1:N},E_{1:N},T_{1:N}), where E1:N=(E1,…,EN)E_{1:N}=(E_{1},\dots,E_{N}), the potential outcome pairs (Yi​(0),Yi​(1))i=1N(Y_{i}(0),Y_{i}(1))_{i=1}^{N} are independent across units. Moreover, for t∈{0,1}t\in\{0,1\}, there exists a common conditional distribution PY⁡(t)|X,EP_{Y(t)\mid X,E} such that, for each i∈{1,…,N}i\in\{1,\dots,N\},

Yi(t)∣(X1:N,E1:N,T1:N)∼PY⁡(t)|X,E(⋅∣Xi,Ei).\displaystyle Y_{i}(t)\mid(X_{1:N},E_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{Y(t)\mid X,E}(\cdot\mid X_{i},E_{i}). (11)
Assumption 5 (Consistency).

For each observed unit ii, the observation YiobsY_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}} equals the potential outcome evaluated at the realized treatment, i.e.,

Yiobs={Yi​(0),if ​Ti=0,Yi​(1),if ​Ti=1.\displaystyle Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\begin{cases}Y_{i}(0),&\text{if }T_{i}=0,\\ Y_{i}(1),&\text{if }T_{i}=1.\end{cases} (12)

Overall, as a result of the observations above, each observation is distributed as

Yiobs∣(X1:N,T1:N,E1:N)∼PY⁡(Ti)|X,E(⋅∣Xi,Ei),\displaystyle Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\mid(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},E_{1:N})\sim P_{Y(T_{i})\mid X,E}(\cdot\mid X_{i},E_{i}), (13)

and the joint distribution of all relevant variables is specified by the following conditional distributions

Xi∼PX,\displaystyle X_{i}\sim P_{X}, (14a)
Ti|Xi∼Bernoulli⁡(π⁡(Xi)),\displaystyle T_{i}\mid X_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi(X_{i})), (14b)
Ei∣(X1:N,T1:N)∼PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xi,ℒi(X1:N,T1:N)),\displaystyle E_{i}\mid(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\!\left(\cdot\mid X_{i},\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right), (14c)
Yi(Ti)∣(X1:N,E1:N,T1:N)∼PY⁡(Ti)|X,E(⋅∣Xi,Ei)\displaystyle Y_{i}(T_{i})\mid(X_{1:N},E_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{Y(T_{i})\mid X,E}(\cdot\mid X_{i},E_{i}) (14d)
Yiobs=Yi​(Ti)\displaystyle Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_{i}(T_{i}) (14e)

Under this joint distribution, variables associated with different units are generally dependent.

2.1 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formalize the individual treatment effect under interference and state the corresponding counterfactual coverage objectives in the transductive and inductive settings. The primary inferential target is the individual treatment effect (ITE), defined as the difference between a unit’s two potential outcomes at the same exposure,

τ=Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0).\displaystyle\tau=Y(1)-Y(0). (15)

Given the observational dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, to be specified differently for the inductive and transductive settings, and a unit with covariates XX and exposure EE, the goal is to construct an ITE prediction set ΓITE​(X,E)\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}}(X,E) satisfying the marginal coverage guarantee

Pr[τ∈ΓITE(X,E)]≥1−α,\displaystyle\Pr[\tau\in\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}}(X,E)]\geq 1-\alpha, (16)

for a user-defined miscoverage level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), where the probability is taken over both the observational data 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the test unit. We consider two instantiations of this requirement.

2.1.1 Transductive ITE Estimation

As illustrated in the left panel of Figure 3, in the transductive setting we are given a dataset 𝒟=((,,,,,,,))i=1N\mathcal{D}=((X_{i},T_{i},E_{i},Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}))_{i=1}^{N} for all NN units, and the goal is to construct a family of prediction sets {ΓiITE}i=1N\{\Gamma_{i}^{\mathrm{ITE}}\}_{i=1}^{N} that cover the ITEs of the observed units on average. Specifically, the transductive ITE coverage requirement is

PrI∼Unif⁡({1,…,N})[YI(1)−YI(0)∈ΓIITE(XI,EI)]≥1−α,\displaystyle\Pr_{I\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{1,\dots,N\})}\hskip-2.5pt\left[Y_{I}(1)-Y_{I}(0)\hskip-1.99997pt\in\hskip-1.99997pt\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{ITE}}(X_{I},E_{I})\right]\hskip-2.5pt\geq\hskip-2.5pt1-\alpha, (17)

where the probability is taken over the random index I∼Unif⁡({1,…,N}){I}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{1,\dots,N\}), as well as over the randomness in the observational dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the potential outcomes.

Since the factual outcome Yi​(Ti)Y_{i}(T_{i}) is observed for every unit, constructing an ITE prediction set reduces to constructing a prediction set for the missing potential outcome Yi​(T¯i)Y_{i}(\bar{T}_{i}), where T¯i=1−Ti\bar{T}_{i}=1-T_{i} denotes the counterfactual treatment. Let ΓiT¯i\Gamma_{i}^{\bar{T}_{i}} denote a prediction set for this missing potential outcome. Combining this set with the observed factual outcome yields the sets

ΓiITE={Γi1−Yi​(0),if ​Ti=0,Yi​(1)−Γi0,if ​Ti=1,\displaystyle\Gamma_{i}^{\mathrm{ITE}}=\begin{cases}\Gamma_{i}^{1}-Y_{i}(0),&\text{if }T_{i}=0,\\ Y_{i}(1)-\Gamma_{i}^{0},&\text{if }T_{i}=1,\end{cases} (18)

where for sets A⊂ℝdA\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and B⊂ℝdB\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have defined the difference set A−B={a−b:a∈A,b∈B}A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,b\in B\}. Consequently, if the counterfactual potential-outcome prediction sets satisfy

PrI∼Unif⁡({1,…,N})[YI(T¯I)∈ΓIT¯I]≥1−α,\displaystyle\Pr_{{I}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{1,\dots,N\})}\left[Y_{I}(\bar{T}_{I})\in\Gamma_{I}^{\bar{T}_{I}}\right]\geq 1-\alpha, (19)

then the induced sets {ΓiITE}i=1N\{\Gamma_{i}^{\mathrm{ITE}}\}_{i=1}^{N} satisfy the transductive ITE coverage requirement in (17).

2.1.2 Inductive ITE Estimation

As illustrated in the right panel of Figure 3, in the inductive setting we are given a dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} including tuples 𝒟={(Xi,Ti,Ei,Yiobs)}i=1N−1\mathcal{D}=\{(X_{i},T_{i},E_{i},Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}})\}_{i=1}^{N-1} for N−1N-1 units, and the goal is to construct a set predictor ΓITE\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}} that covers the ITE of a new unit with covariates XN∼PXX_{N}\sim P_{X} and an exposure level ENE_{N} given by the exposure that this unit would have experienced in the network of NN interfering units whose first N−1N-1 units have covariates and treatments as in 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Formally, the output of inductive ITE estimation is a set predictor ΓITE\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}} satisfying the marginal coverage guarantee

Pr[YN(1)−YN(0)∈ΓITE(XN,EN)]≥1−α,\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{N}(1)-Y_{N}(0)\in\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}}(X_{N},E_{N})\right]\geq 1-\alpha, (20)

where the probability is over the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the test unit (XN,EN,YN​(0),YN​(1))(X_{N},E_{N},Y_{N}(0),Y_{N}(1)). Unlike in the transductive setting, neither potential outcome is observed for the test unit NN. Therefore, the ITE prediction set ΓITE​(XN,EN)\Gamma^{\mathrm{ITE}}(X_{N},E_{N}) must be constructed from prediction sets Γ0​(XN,EN)\Gamma^{0}(X_{N},E_{N}) and Γ1​(XN,EN)\Gamma^{1}(X_{N},E_{N}) for both potential outcomes.

In the following, we detail the proposed solution for the transductive setting, and present its counterpart for inductive inference, which follows the same principles, in Appendix F.

3 Transductive Interference-Adjusted Weighted Conformal Prediction

In this section, we introduce IA-WCP for the transductive setting. Without loss of generality, we condition on the event that the randomly selected test unit I∼Unif⁡({1,…,N})I\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\{1,\dots,N\}) is a control unit, i.e., TI=0T_{I}=0, and construct a prediction set for its missing treated potential outcome YI​(1)Y_{I}(1). In what follows, we suppress the dependence on the target treatment in the notation whenever it is clear from context.

3.1 Weighted Conformal Prediction

We first review conventional WCP for counterfactual outcomes (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Lei and Candès, 2021) and explain why it is generally invalid under interference. Following the construction in (Lei and Candès, 2021), let S:𝒳×ℰ×𝒴→ℝS:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} be a fixed nonconformity scoring function. For every treated calibration unit j∈ℐ1j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, define the observational calibration score Vjobs=S⁡(Xj,Ej,Yj​(1))V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}=S(X_{j},E_{j},Y_{j}(1)), and, for a candidate value y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} and test unit II, define the test score VI​(y)=S⁡(XI,EI,y)V_{I}(y)=S(X_{I},E_{I},y).

To correct for the covariate shift induced by treatment assignment, WCP (Tibshirani et al., 2019; Lei and Candès, 2021) assigns to each unit j∈ℐ1∪{I}j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\} the propensity-ratio-based weight

Wj=1−π⁡(Xj)π⁡(Xj),\displaystyle W_{j}=\frac{1-\pi(X_{j})}{\pi(X_{j})}, (21)

and it defines the observational conformal pp-value as

pI,yobs=WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj𝟙{Vjobs≥VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (22)

Finally, the prediction set is constructed as

ΓIWCP={y∈𝒴:pI,yobs>α}.\displaystyle\Gamma_{I}^{\rm WCP}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>\alpha\}. (23)

As proved in (Lei and Candès, 2021), the marginal coverage guarantee in (19) holds for the missing potential outcome YI​(1)Y_{I}(1) under the standard SUTVA. In fact, in this case, the discrepancy between the distributions of calibration and test scores is fully accounted for by the covariates, and the weights in (21) compensate for this shift. Under network interference, however, a residual discrepancy may remain through the exposure variables, even after correcting for covariate shift.

3.2 Transductive IA-WCP

Define the set of treated calibration units whose neighborhoods contain the test unit II as

ℋI={j∈ℐ1:I∈𝒩j(X1:N)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{I}=\left\{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}:I\in\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N})\right\}. (24)

IA-WCP modifies the WCP prediction set (23) as

ΓIIA−WCP={y∈𝒴:pI,yobs>(α−ρI,y)+},\displaystyle\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>(\alpha-\rho_{I,y})_{+}\right\}, (25)

where (x)+=max⁡{x,0}(x)_{+}=\max\{x,0\} and

ρI,y=∑j∈ℋIWj𝟙{Vjobs<VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle\rho_{I,y}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (26)

The correction ρI,y\rho_{I,y} is the fraction of total conformal weight assigned to the affected calibration units whose observational score lies below the candidate test score. Intuitively, this term captures the discrepancy between calibration and test scores caused by the presence of network interference. In particular, note that, in the absence of interference, we have ℋI=∅\mathcal{H}_{I}=\emptyset and ρI,y=0\rho_{I,y}=0 for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, and the prediction set ΓIIA−WCP\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}} reduces to the WCP set (Lei and Candès, 2021) in (23).

The following result shows that the correction term (26) is sufficient to restore the marginal guarantee (19).

Theorem 1.

Under Assumptions 1–5, for a randomly chosen control unit II, the IA-WCP set ΓIIA−WCP\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}} in (25) satisfies the inequality

Pr⁡[YI​(1)∉ΓIIA−WCP|TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\notin\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\Big|T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (27)
Proof.

See Appendix C. ∎

When TI=1T_{I}=1, the analogous construction uses the control units as the calibration sample and the reverse propensity-ratio weights Wj=π⁡(Xj)/(1−π⁡(Xj))W_{j}=\pi(X_{j})/(1-\pi(X_{j})), ensuring that the resulting set (18) satisfies the desired condition (17).

To explain the rationale behind the correction term (26) introduced by IA-WCP, we outline the main steps in the proof of Theorem 1. First, we condition on the event

Aℐ1,I={Tj=1 for\displaystyle A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}=\big\{T_{j}=1\text{ for } j∈ℐ1,TI=0,\displaystyle j\in\mathcal{I}_{1},T_{I}=0,
Tj=0 for j∉ℐ1∪{I}},\displaystyle T_{j}=0\text{ for }j\notin\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}\big\}, (28)

which states that unit II is a control unit and that ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} is the set of treated units. As ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} ranges over all subsets of {1,…,N}∖{I}\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{I\}, the events Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I} form a disjoint partition of {TI=0}\{T_{I}=0\}. It therefore suffices to establish (27) conditionally on each event Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I} and then apply the law of total probability.

Conditional on Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}, as shown in Appendix C.1, the covariates (Xj)j∈ℐ1∪{I}(X_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}} are weighted exchangeable with the weights in (21). This is the key fact underlying the validity of WCP in the absence of interference.

In the presence of interference, however, this does not imply the weighted exchangeability of the calibration and test scores due to the dependence of the outcomes on the exposure variables. In particular, conditional on Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I} and X1:NX_{1:N}, the joint distribution p((Yj(1),Ej)j∈ℐ1∪{I}∣Aℐ1,I,X1:N)p\left((Y_{j}(1),E_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I},X_{1:N}\right) need not be invariant under permutations that exchange unit II with a calibration unit.

IA-WCP rests on the observation that this source of non-exchangeability disappears under a modified interventional distribution in which the treatment of unit II is changed to one. In fact, denoting the resulting exposures and potential outcomes by (E~jI)j∈ℐ1∪{I}(\tilde{E}_{j}^{I})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}} and (Y~jI​(1))j∈ℐ1∪{I}(\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1))_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}}, respectively, their conditional joint distribution p((Y~jI(1),E~jI)j∈ℐ1∪{I}∣Aℐ1,I,X1:N,do(TI=1))p\left((\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1),\tilde{E}_{j}^{I})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I},X_{1:N},\operatorname{do}(T_{I}=1)\right) can be shown to be exchangeable under permutations of test and calibration units (see Appendix C.1). Combined with the weighted exchangeability of the covariates, this implies that the prediction set

Γ~IWCP={y∈𝒴:pI,yint>α},\displaystyle\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\rm WCP}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}>\alpha\}, (29)

built using the interventional conformal pp-value

pI,yint=WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj𝟙{Vjint≥VIint(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj,\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{{W}_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}{W}_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{I}^{\mathrm{int}}(y)\}}{{W}_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}{W}_{j}}, (30)

with scores Vjint=S⁡(Xj,E~jI,Y~jI​(1))V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}=S(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I},\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)) for j∈ℐ1j\in\mathcal{I}_{1} and VIint​(y)=S⁡(XI,E~II,y)V_{I}^{\mathrm{int}}(y)=S(X_{I},\tilde{E}^{I}_{I},y) satisfies the marginal coverage guarantee.

Lemma 1.

Under Assumptions 1–5, for a randomly chosen control unit II, the ideal WCP set Γ~IWCP\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\rm WCP} in (29) satisfies the inequality

Pr⁡[YI​(1)∉Γ~IWCP|TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\notin\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\rm WCP}\Big|T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (31)
Proof.

See Appendix C.1. ∎

The last step of the proof of Theorem 1 is to show that it is possible to construct a coupling of the observational and interventional vectors of nonconformity scores, that is, a joint distribution whose marginals coincide with their respective observational and interventional distributions, such that for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, the following bound holds

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,y,a.s.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y},\quad\text{a.s.} (32)

The correction term ρI,y\rho_{I,y} in (26) then accounts for the discrepancy between the observable and interventional conformal pp-values, ensuring that the set ΓIIA−WCP\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}} includes Γ~IWCP\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\rm WCP} almost surely, and completing the proof of Theorem 1.

3.3 Transductive IA-WCP+

The correction in (26) is worst-case, as it is derived without imposing any restriction on how the observational and interventional nonconformity scores of the affected units may differ. Appendix D provides an example in which the correction is tight in terms of marginal coverage, in the sense that the prediction sets induced by the ideal interventional and corrected observational pp-values have identical marginal coverage. In many applications, however, changing the treatment of one unit induces only a bounded perturbation in the nonconformity scores of the affected units. We denote a bound on the perturbation in the score of unit jj caused by changing the treatment of unit II by the scalar ΔjI\Delta_{j}^{I}, which is formally defined in Appendix E. Under the technical assumptions stated therein, this bound yields a sharper correction that accounts for the magnitude of the score perturbation

ρI,y+=∑j∈ℋIWj𝟙{VI(y)−ΔjI≤Vjobs<VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle\rho_{I,y}^{+}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\left\{V_{I}(y)-\Delta_{j}^{I}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\right\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (33)

Replacing (26) with (33) yields a stability-aware variant of IA-WCP, which we call IA-WCP+. As shown in Appendix E, IA-WCP+ preserves the coverage requirement (27) under the mentioned technical assumptions.

4 Experiments

We evaluate the proposed methods using a synthetic peer-interference model inspired by (Forastiere et al., 2021; Chin, 2019). Appendix H provides additional results for this setting, along with experiments in a wireless traffic-slicing problem (Foukas et al., 2017; Bao et al., 2017).

4.1 Setup

We consider a network of N=300N=300 units in which each unit ii has covariate Xi=(Ui,Gi)X_{i}=(U_{i},G_{i}), where Ui∼Unif⁡[−1,1]U_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1] and Gi∼Unif⁡{1,…,G}G_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{1,\ldots,G\} is a group label. Treatments are drawn independently according to Ti|Xi∼Bernoulli⁡(σ⁡(Ui/2))T_{i}\mid X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\sigma(U_{i}/2)), and the neighborhood of unit ii contains its same-group peers, 𝒩i(X1:N)={j≠i:Gj=Gi}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{j\neq i:G_{j}=G_{i}\}. The exposure is given by the fraction of treated units in the same group, i.e.,

Ei=∑j∈𝒩i(X1:N)Tj|𝒩i(X1:N)|,\displaystyle E_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})}T_{j}}{|\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})|}, (34)

with the convention that Ei=0E_{i}=0 if 𝒩i(X1:N)=∅\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\emptyset. The potential outcomes are

Yi​(0)\displaystyle Y_{i}(0) =0,\displaystyle=0, (35)
Yi​(1)\displaystyle Y_{i}(1) =θ​Ui+[σ⁡(λ⁡(Ei−0.5))−σ⁡(−0.5​λ)]+εi,\displaystyle=\theta U_{i}+\left[\sigma(\lambda(E_{i}-0.5))-\sigma(-0.5\lambda)\right]+\varepsilon_{i}, (36)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) denotes the sigmoid function and εi∼𝒩⁡(0,σε2)\varepsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}). This model captures a simple peer-effect mechanism in which each unit responds to the treatment rate in its group, with the response becoming stronger once peer adoption crosses 50%. Such a mechanism can represent settings with social reinforcement or congestion effects. Unless specified otherwise, we instantiate the model with G=16G=16 groups, linear coefficient θ=0.25\theta=0.25, sigmoid parameter λ=10\lambda=10, and noise standard deviation σε=0.05\sigma_{\varepsilon}=0.05.

4.2 Benchmarks

We use the absolute-residual score and compare WCP (Lei and Candès, 2021), ideal WCP based on the unobservable interventional pp-value in (30), and the proposed IA-WCP and IA-WCP+. Ideal WCP serves as an oracle reference, and it is available here because the data-generating mechanism is known. We apply these calibration methods to three different base predictors. The first is the interference-free linear predictor Y^​(1)=θ​U\hat{Y}(1)=\theta U, which returns the mean outcome in the absence of interference. We also consider two fitted linear predictors, a covariate-only predictor Y^​(1)=θ^U​U+θ^0\hat{Y}(1)=\hat{\theta}_{U}U+\hat{\theta}_{0}, and an exposure-aware predictor Y^​(1)=θ^E​E+θ^U​U+θ^0\hat{Y}(1)=\hat{\theta}_{E}E+\hat{\theta}_{U}U+\hat{\theta}_{0}. The two linear predictors are fitted on treated units from ten independent training networks.

For IA-WCP+, the stability margin is given by

ΔjI=(λ4+|θ^E|)​|E~jI−Ej|,\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{I}=\left(\frac{\lambda}{4}+|\hat{\theta}_{E}|\right)\left|\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}-E_{j}\right|, (37)

where θ^E\hat{\theta}_{E} is set to zero for predictors that do not use the exposure level EE.

4.3 Results

We first study the effect of neighborhood size by varying the number of groups GG. As shown in Figure 4, smaller values of GG produce larger neighborhoods and increase the fraction of calibration units affected by the intervention. In this regime, WCP undercovers with the miscoverage gap increasing as the number of groups GG decreases. For example, at G=4G=4, its empirical coverage is approximately 0.750.75, below the target level 0.80.8. Across all values of GG, ideal WCP and the proposed IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ attain or exceed the desired coverage level. However, because IA-WCP uses a worst-case correction, it becomes highly conservative for small values of GG. In contrast, IA-WCP+ performance tracks that of ideal WCP and is substantially more efficient than IA-WCP.

We next investigate how the choice of base predictor affects coverage and efficiency. Figure 5 shows that replacing the interference-free linear predictor with predictors fitted on data generated under interference substantially reduces prediction-set width. It also reduces the empirical miscoverage gap of WCP, whose coverage approaches that of ideal WCP when the predictor accounts for the exposure level. It is important to highlight that this behavior is specific to the present experiment, as conventional WCP lacks a general coverage guarantee under interference. The proposed methods retain their validity across all three predictors. Moreover, IA-WCP+ is noticeably narrower than IA-WCP when using the interference-free linear predictor or covariate-only predictor. When exposure EE is included in the predictor, the additional term |θ^E||\hat{\theta}_{E}| enlarges the stability margin (37), causing IA-WCP+ to nearly coincide with IA-WCP.

5 Conclusion

We studied conformal counterfactual prediction for individual potential outcomes and treatment effects under interference in the inductive and transductive settings. In either setting, a unit’s potential outcomes may depend on the covariates and treatment assignments of other units, creating a source of non-exchangeability that is not corrected by standard unit-level propensity weighting and may invalidate existing conformal methods.

To address this challenge, we have developed two interference-adjusted calibration methods. The first, IA-WCP, retains finite-sample marginal coverage under interference by adjusting the observational conformal pp-value using a worst-case bound on the discrepancy between observational and interventional calibration scores. Although this correction remains valid under arbitrary score perturbations, it can produce conservative prediction sets. When bounds on intervention-induced score perturbations are available, IA-WCP+ uses them to sharpen the correction and improve efficiency while retaining the same coverage guarantee. Our experiments show that conventional WCP can remain close to nominal coverage when interference is weak, but it may undercover as interference becomes stronger. In contrast, IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ maintain the target coverage, with IA-WCP+ generally producing smaller prediction sets.

Conformal Individual Treatment Effect Estimation under Networked Interference: Supplementary Materials

 

Appendix A Related Work

Conformal Inference for Treatment Effects.

Conformal prediction (CP) is a calibration framework that transforms point predictions into prediction sets with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees, provided that the calibration and test data are exchangeable (Shafer and Vovk, 2008). In counterfactual inference, however, exchangeability is typically violated because outcomes under a given treatment are observed only for units assigned to that treatment, inducing covariate shift between the calibration and test distributions. WCP addresses this shift by reweighting the calibration data (Tibshirani et al., 2019). Under the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA), unconfoundedness, and overlap, WCP constructs valid prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes and individual treatment effects (ITEs) under covariate-dependent treatment assignment (Lei and Candès, 2021).

Subsequent work has relaxed these assumptions in several directions. Sensitivity analysis has been introduced to address potential violations of unconfoundedness (Jin et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024); interventional data have been leveraged to mitigate hidden confounding (Chen et al., 2024; Qchohi et al., 2026); and synthetic-powered prediction has been proposed to reduce the inefficiency caused by poor overlap (Farzaneh et al., 2025). However, all these methods fundamentally rely on the no-interference assumption embedded in SUTVA. In this work, we relax this assumption and construct valid conformal prediction sets for counterfactual outcomes and ITEs under network interference.

Causal inference under interference.

The causal-inference literature relaxes the no-interference component of SUTVA by imposing structure on how one unit’s treatment may affect another unit’s outcome. Early work studies direct and spillover effects under partial interference, where interference is restricted to known groups (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Tchetgen and VanderWeele, 2012). Exposure mappings extend this framework to richer interference patterns by summarizing the treatment assignments of other units through an exposure variable, thereby enabling the identification and estimation of causal effects under randomized or observational treatment assignment (Aronow and Samii, 2017; Forastiere et al., 2021). More recent machine-learning approaches exploit network structure to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects, exposure-response functions, and treatment policies in networked populations (Ma and Tresp, 2021; Huang et al., 2023b). These works have primarily focused on defining causal estimands and estimating population-level or heterogeneous effects under interference. In contrast, we focus on constructing model-agnostic, finite-sample prediction sets for individual potential outcomes and treatment effects.

Conformal Prediction on Networked Data.

A growing body of literature adapts conformal prediction to graph-structured observations. For node-level prediction, existing methods use graph neighborhoods to reweight nonconformity scores (Clarkson, 2023; H. Zargarbashi et al., 2023), or learn topology-aware corrections that exploit permutation invariance to preserve marginal validity (Huang et al., 2023a). Related work addresses the distribution shift induced when new nodes or edges enter an inductive graph (H. Zargarbashi and Bojchevski, 2024), and extends conformal uncertainty quantification to link prediction (Zhao et al., 2024). In these settings, the graph structure is leveraged to learn node representations and improve calibration efficiency. However, the target remains an unobserved label or edge in the factual graph, rather than a counterfactual outcome under a treatment intervention. The closest work to ours is that of Zhou et al. (2025), which exploits a fixed transductive network to learn representations that account for hidden confounding, adapts conformal calibration to node degree, and estimates ITEs. Nevertheless, the framework in (Zhou et al., 2025) explicitly assumes no network interference, whereas in our setting, treatment spillover across neighboring nodes directly alters the target counterfactual outcomes.

Appendix B Examples of Permutation-equivariant Neighborhood and Exposure Maps

We now list several permutation-equivariant neighborhood rules and deterministic exposure maps satisfying Assumption 2. These maps induce degenerate exposure kernels of the form

PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xi,ℒi(X1:N,T1:N))=δei(X1:N,T−i1:N)(⋅),\displaystyle P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{i},\mathcal{L}_{i}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right)=\delta_{e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})}(\cdot), (38)

where ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N}) denotes the exposure assigned to unit ii, and δx​(⋅)\delta_{x}(\cdot) denotes the Dirac measure centered at xx.

Throughout this section we use the same permutation convention as in Assumption 2. For a permutation σ\sigma of {1,…,N}\{1,\ldots,N\}, we denote the permuted treatment and covariate vectors by

Tσ⁡(1:N)=(Tσ⁡(1),…,Tσ⁡(N)),Xσ⁡(1:N)=(Xσ⁡(1),…,Xσ⁡(N)).\displaystyle T_{\sigma(1:N)}=(T_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,T_{\sigma(N)}),\qquad X_{\sigma(1:N)}=(X_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,X_{\sigma(N)}). (39)

Thus, under the relabeled vectors (Tσ⁡(1:N),Xσ⁡(1:N))(T_{\sigma(1:N)},X_{\sigma(1:N)}), the unit at position ii corresponds to the original unit σ⁡(i)\sigma(i). A deterministic exposure map is permutation-equivariant if, for every permutation σ\sigma and every i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N,

ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (40)
  1. 1.

    Global treated-count exposure. Set 𝒩i(X1:N)={1,…,N}∖{i}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\} and define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=∑j≠iTj.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\sum_{j\neq i}T_{j}. (41)

    Then, for any permutation σ\sigma,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=∑ℓ≠iTσ⁡(ℓ)=∑j≠σ⁡(i)Tj=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\sum_{\ell\neq i}T_{\sigma(\ell)}=\sum_{j\neq\sigma(i)}T_{j}=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (42)
  2. 2.

    Fraction treated outside unit ii. Again set 𝒩i(X1:N)={1,…,N}∖{i}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\} and define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=1N−1∑j≠iTj.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq i}T_{j}. (43)

    Then, for any permutation σ\sigma,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=1N−1∑ℓ≠iTσ⁡(ℓ)=1N−1∑j≠σ⁡(i)Tj=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{\ell\neq i}T_{\sigma(\ell)}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq\sigma(i)}T_{j}=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (44)
  3. 3.

    kk-nearest-neighbor treated-count exposure. Let d:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} be a distance, and let 𝒩i(k)(X1:N)\mathcal{N}_{i}^{(k)}(X_{1:N}) denote the set of indices corresponding to the kk nearest neighbors of unit ii among {1,…,N}∖{i}\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\}. We assume either that ties occur with probability zero, or that they are resolved by a permutation-equivariant rule. Define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=∑j∈𝒩i(k)(X1:N)Tj.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{(k)}(X_{1:N})}T_{j}. (45)

    Under the permutation convention above, the nearest-neighbor set satisfies

    𝒩i(k)(Xσ⁡(1:N))={σ−1(j):j∈𝒩σ⁡(i)(k)(X1:N)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}^{(k)}(X_{\sigma(1:N)})=\{\sigma^{-1}(j):j\in\mathcal{N}_{\sigma(i)}^{(k)}(X_{1:N})\}. (46)

    Therefore,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=∑ℓ∈𝒩i(k)(Xσ⁡(1:N))Tσ⁡(ℓ)=∑j∈𝒩σ⁡(i)(k)(X1:N)Tj=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{(k)}(X_{\sigma(1:N)})}\hskip-20.00003ptT_{\sigma(\ell)}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{\sigma(i)}^{(k)}(X_{1:N})}\hskip-15.00002ptT_{j}=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (47)
  4. 4.

    Radius-based treated-count exposure. Let d:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ+d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{+} be a distance and fix r>0r>0. Set

    𝒩i(X1:N)={j≠i:d(Xi,Xj)≤r},\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{j\neq i:d(X_{i},X_{j})\leq r\}, (48)

    and define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=∑j∈𝒩i(X1:N)Tj.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})}T_{j}. (49)

    Then, for any permutation σ\sigma,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=∑ℓ≠iTσ⁡(ℓ)𝟙{d(Xσ⁡(i),Xσ⁡(ℓ))≤r}\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\sum_{\ell\neq i}T_{\sigma(\ell)}\mathds{1}\{d(X_{\sigma(i)},X_{\sigma(\ell)})\leq r\} =∑j≠σ⁡(i)Tj𝟙{d(Xσ⁡(i),Xj)≤r}\displaystyle=\sum_{j\neq\sigma(i)}T_{j}\mathds{1}\{d(X_{\sigma(i)},X_{j})\leq r\}
    =eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (50)
  5. 5.

    Weighted exposure. Let a:𝒳×𝒳→ℝa:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} be a measurable weight function. Set 𝒩i(X1:N)={1,…,N}∖{i}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\} and define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=∑j≠ia(Xi,Xj)Tj.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\sum_{j\neq i}a(X_{i},X_{j})T_{j}. (51)

    Then, for any permutation σ\sigma,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=∑ℓ≠ia(Xσ⁡(i),Xσ⁡(ℓ))Tσ⁡(ℓ)\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\hskip-1.99997pt\sum_{\ell\neq i}a(X_{\sigma(i)},X_{\sigma(\ell)})T_{\sigma(\ell)} =∑j≠σ⁡(i)a(Xσ⁡(i),Xj)Tj=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle=\hskip-1.99997pt\sum_{j\neq\sigma(i)}a(X_{\sigma(i)},X_{j})T_{j}=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (52)
  6. 6.

    Threshold exposure. Let m∈{1,…,N−1}m\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}, set 𝒩i(X1:N)={1,…,N}∖{i}\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{i\}, and define

    ei(X1:N,T1:N−i)=𝟙{∑j≠iTj≥m}.\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{1:N},T^{-i}_{1:N})=\mathds{1}\left\{\sum_{j\neq i}T_{j}\geq m\right\}. (53)

    Since the treated count outside unit ii is permutation-equivariant,

    ei(Xσ⁡(1:N),Tσ⁡(1:N)−i)=𝟙{∑ℓ≠iTσ⁡(ℓ)≥m}=𝟙{∑j≠σ⁡(i)Tj≥m}=eσ⁡(i)(X1:N,T1:N−σ⁡(i)).\displaystyle e_{i}(X_{\sigma(1:N)},T^{-i}_{\sigma(1:N)})=\mathds{1}\left\{\sum_{\ell\neq i}T_{\sigma(\ell)}\geq m\right\}=\mathds{1}\left\{\sum_{j\neq\sigma(i)}T_{j}\geq m\right\}=e_{\sigma(i)}(X_{1:N},T^{-\sigma(i)}_{1:N}). (54)

Appendix C Proof of Transductive IA-WCP Validity

We prove the result for the case in which the test unit II satisfies TI=0T_{I}=0, so that the missing potential outcome is YI​(1)Y_{I}(1). The case TI=1T_{I}=1 is analogous. All probabilities in the remainder of this proof are conditional on TI=0T_{I}=0.

We first establish weighted exchangeability of the interventional sample and the validity of the ideal WCP procedure under interference. We then compare the observational and interventional pp-values under a joint coupling and conclude the validity proof of IA-WCP.

C.1 Validity of the ideal WCP procedure

Let T~I1:N\tilde{T}^{I}_{1:N} denote the treatment vector obtained by setting the treatment of unit II to one while leaving all other treatment assignments in T1:NT_{1:N} unchanged, i.e.,

T~II=1,T~jI=Tj,j≠I.\displaystyle\tilde{T}^{I}_{I}=1,\qquad\tilde{T}^{I}_{j}=T_{j},\quad j\neq I. (55)

Under this intervention, let E~jI\tilde{E}_{j}^{I} denote the exposure of unit jj, and let Y~jI​(1)\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1) denote the corresponding treated potential outcome. Define

Z~j=(Xj,E~jI,Y~jI(1)),j=1,…,N.\displaystyle\tilde{Z}_{j}=(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I},\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)),\qquad j=1,\dots,N. (56)

We now show that, for any treatment vector T1:NT_{1:N} such that TI=0T_{I}=0, the augmented interventional sample

𝒟~1=(Z~j)j∈ℐ1∪{I},\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{1}=(\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}}, (57)

is weighted exchangeable.

Lemma 2 (Weighted exchangeability of the interventional sample).

Fix an index II and a treated calibration set ℐ1⊆{1,…,N}∖{I}\mathcal{I}_{1}\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\setminus\{I\}, and let 𝒮=ℐ1∪{I}\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{I\}. Work conditionally on the observational assignment event

Aℐ1,I={Tj=1 for j∈ℐ1,TI=0,Tj=0 for j∉𝒮}.\displaystyle A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}=\{T_{j}=1\text{ for }j\in\mathcal{I}_{1},T_{I}=0,T_{j}=0\text{ for }j\notin\mathcal{S}\}. (58)

The intervention is applied after conditioning on this observational assignment event.

Under Assumptions 1–5, the conditional density of (Z~j)j∈𝒮(\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}} admits the decomposition

p⁡((Z~j)j∈𝒮∣Aℐ1,I)=c​w​(XI)​g​((Z~j)j∈𝒮),\displaystyle p\bigl((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\bigr)=cw(X_{I})g\bigl((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\bigr), (59)

where c>0c>0,

w⁡(x)=1−π⁡(x)π⁡(x),\displaystyle w(x)=\frac{1-\pi(x)}{\pi(x)}, (60)

and gg is invariant under permutations of the arguments indexed by 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

Proof.

By Assumption 1,

Pr(Aℐ1,I∣X1:N)=∏j∈ℐ1π(Xj)(1−π(XI))∏j∉𝒮(1−π(Xj)).\displaystyle\Pr(A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\mid X_{1:N})=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}\pi(X_{j})\bigl(1-\pi(X_{I})\bigr)\prod_{j\notin\mathcal{S}}\bigl(1-\pi(X_{j})\bigr). (61)

Therefore,

p(X1:N∣Aℐ1,I)\displaystyle p(X_{1:N}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}) =Pr(Aℐ1,I∣X1:N)pX⊗N(X1:N)Pr⁡(Aℐ1,I)\displaystyle=\frac{\Pr(A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\mid X_{1:N})p_{X}^{\otimes N}(X_{1:N})}{\Pr(A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I})}
=c0​∏j∈ℐ1π⁡(Xj)​pX​(Xj)​(1−π⁡(XI))​pX​(XI)​∏j∉𝒮(1−π⁡(Xj))​pX​(Xj),\displaystyle=c_{0}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}\pi(X_{j})p_{X}(X_{j})\bigl(1-\pi(X_{I})\bigr)p_{X}(X_{I})\prod_{j\notin\mathcal{S}}\bigl(1-\pi(X_{j})\bigr)p_{X}(X_{j}), (62)

where c0=1/Pr⁡(Aℐ1,I)c_{0}=1/\Pr(A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}). Multiplying and dividing the factor associated with II by π⁡(XI)\pi(X_{I}) gives

p(X1:N∣Aℐ1,I)=c0w(XI)∏j∈𝒮π(Xj)pX(Xj)∏j∉𝒮(1−π(Xj))pX(Xj).\displaystyle p(X_{1:N}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I})=c_{0}w(X_{I})\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(X_{j})p_{X}(X_{j})\prod_{j\notin\mathcal{S}}\bigl(1-\pi(X_{j})\bigr)p_{X}(X_{j}). (63)

Integrating out the covariates indexed by 𝒮c\mathcal{S}^{c} contributes only a constant independent of (Xj)j∈𝒮(X_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}. The resulting marginal density is therefore proportional to

w⁡(XI)​∏j∈𝒮π⁡(Xj)​pX​(Xj),\displaystyle w(X_{I})\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(X_{j})p_{X}(X_{j}), (64)

which proves the weighted exchangeability of covariates conditioned on the event Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}.

We now define the interventional variables using the intervened treatment vector T~I\tilde{T}^{I}. Conditionally on (X1:N,T~I)(X_{1:N},\tilde{T}^{I}), Assumption 3 gives

p(E~1:NI∣X1:N,Aℐ1,I,do(TI=1))=∏j=1NpE|X,ℒ(E~jI∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T~1:NI)).\displaystyle p(\tilde{E}_{1:N}^{I}\mid X_{1:N},A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I},\operatorname{do}(T_{I}=1))=\prod_{j=1}^{N}p_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},\tilde{T}^{I}_{1:N})\right). (65)

Similarly, by Assumption 4,

p(Y~1:NI(1)∣X1:N,E~1:NI,Aℐ1,I,do(TI=1))=∏j=1NpY⁡(1)|X,E(Y~jI(1)∣Xj,E~jI).\displaystyle p\left(\tilde{Y}_{1:N}^{I}(1)\mid X_{1:N},\tilde{E}_{1:N}^{I},A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I},\operatorname{do}(T_{I}=1)\right)=\prod_{j=1}^{N}p_{Y(1)\mid X,E}\left(\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)\mid X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}\right). (66)

Combining (63), (65), and (66), and then marginalizing over all variables indexed by 𝒮c={1,…,N}∖𝒮\mathcal{S}^{c}=\{1,\dots,N\}\setminus\mathcal{S}, yields

p⁡((Z~j)j∈𝒮∣Aℐ1,I)=c​w​(XI)​g​((Z~j)j∈𝒮),\displaystyle p\bigl((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\mid A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\bigr)=cw(X_{I})g\bigl((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\bigr), (67)

for a normalizing constant c>0c>0, where gg collects all remaining factors after the extraction of w⁡(XI)w(X_{I}).

It remains to show that gg is invariant under permutations of its arguments. Let σ\sigma be any permutation of the indices in 𝒮\mathcal{S}, extended to {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\} by setting σ⁡(k)=k\sigma(k)=k for k∉𝒮k\notin\mathcal{S}. The factors

∏j∈𝒮π⁡(Xj)​pX​(Xj)\displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\pi(X_{j})p_{X}(X_{j}) (68)

and

∏j∈𝒮pY⁡(1)|X,E​(Y~jI​(1)∣Xj,E~jI)\displaystyle\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}}p_{Y(1)\mid X,E}\left(\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)\mid X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}\right) (69)

are invariant under permutations of the triples

(Xj,E~jI,Y~jI​(1)),j∈𝒮.\displaystyle(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I},\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)),\qquad j\in\mathcal{S}. (70)

Finally, under T~I\tilde{T}^{I}, all units in 𝒮\mathcal{S} have treatment equal to one. Hence a permutation of the labels in 𝒮\mathcal{S} only relabels units with the same intervened treatment. By Assumption 2, the neighborhood rule is permutation equivariant and the exposure kernel is invariant to the ordering of the neighbors, so the joint exposure density is unchanged under the same simultaneous permutation of the covariates, exposures, and outcomes indexed by 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The variables indexed by 𝒮c\mathcal{S}^{c} are integrated out, and the integration measure is invariant under this relabeling.

Therefore gg is invariant under permutations of the arguments (Z~j)j∈𝒮(\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{S}}, proving the claimed decomposition. ∎

By Lemma 2, conditionally on Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}, the augmented interventional sample is weighted exchangeable. Therefore, the standard weighted conformal validity argument (Tibshirani et al., 2019) gives

Pr⁡[pI,Y~II​(1)int≤α|Aℐ1,I]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[p_{I,\tilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\middle|A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\right]\leq\alpha. (71)

This establishes conditional validity at the interventional target outcome Y~II​(1)\widetilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1). Because I∉𝒩I(X1:N)I\notin\mathcal{N}_{I}(X_{1:N}), changing TIT_{I} does not alter the exposure law of the target unit. Under Assumptions 3 and 4, conditionally on Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}, we may therefore couple the target variables so that

(E~II,Y~II​(1))=(EI,YI​(1))a.s.,\displaystyle(\widetilde{E}_{I}^{I},\widetilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1))=(E_{I},Y_{I}(1))\qquad\text{a.s.}, (72)

while preserving their joint law with the interventional calibration scores. Consequently,

Pr⁡[pI,YI​(1)int≤α|Aℐ1,I]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\,\middle|\,A_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}\right]\leq\alpha. (73)

For each fixed II, the events Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}, indexed by ℐ1⊆{1,…,N}∖{I}\mathcal{I}_{1}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{I\}, form a partition of {TI=0}\{T_{I}=0\}. Applying the law of total probability over this partition and then averaging over the selected index II proves Lemma 1.

C.2 Coupling comparison

For this proof, we consider the exposure-law affected set

ℋIex={j∈ℐ1:\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}=\Bigl\{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}: PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T1:N))≠PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T~1:NI))},\displaystyle P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right)\neq P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},\tilde{T}^{I}_{1:N})\right)\Bigr\}, (74)

and write 𝒰Iex=ℐ1∖ℋIex\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}. Note that ℋIex⊆ℋI\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{I} because the conditional exposure law of unit jj is unchanged when I∉𝒩j(X1:N)I\notin\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N}). Thus, proving the comparison first with the set ℋIex\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}} yields the main-text bound by enlarging the index set of the nonnegative correction sum from ℋIex\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}} to ℋI\mathcal{H}_{I}.

Lemma 3.

Under Assumptions 3 and 4, conditionally on TI=0T_{I}=0, the observational conformal pp-value in (22) and the interventional conformal pp-value in (30) admit a coupling such that, simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,yexa.s.,\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho^{\rm ex}_{I,y}\qquad\text{a.s.}, (75)

where

ρI,yex=∑j∈ℋIexWj𝟙{Vjobs<VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle\rho^{\rm ex}_{I,y}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (76)
Proof.

We construct the coupling conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N,I)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I), with TI=0T_{I}=0. Since the exposure of a unit does not depend on its own treatment,

EI∣X1:N,T1:N=𝑑E~II∣X1:N,T~I1:N,\displaystyle E_{I}\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N}\overset{d}{=}\tilde{E}_{I}^{I}\mid X_{1:N},\tilde{T}^{I}_{1:N}, (77)

where =𝑑\overset{d}{=} denotes equality in distribution. Moreover, for every j∈𝒰Iexj\in\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}, the definition of 𝒰Iex\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}} gives

Ej∣X1:N,T1:N=𝑑E~jI∣X1:N,T~I1:N.\displaystyle E_{j}\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N}\overset{d}{=}\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}\mid X_{1:N},\tilde{T}^{I}_{1:N}. (78)

We may therefore couple these exposures so that

EI=E~II, and Ej=E~jI,j∈𝒰Iex,\displaystyle E_{I}=\tilde{E}_{I}^{I},\quad\text{ and }\quad E_{j}=\tilde{E}_{j}^{I},\qquad j\in\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}, (79)

almost surely. Conditional on these coupled exposures, the corresponding treated potential outcomes have the same conditional distribution PY⁡(1)|X,EP_{Y(1)\mid X,E}. Hence, they may be coupled so that

YI​(1)=Y~II​(1), and Yj​(1)=Y~jI​(1),j∈𝒰Iex,\displaystyle Y_{I}(1)=\tilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1),\quad\text{ and }\quad Y_{j}(1)=\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1),\qquad j\in\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}, (80)

almost surely. For every j∈ℋIexj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}, choose any coupling with the correct observational and interventional marginals.

By Assumptions 3 and 4, the unit-specific exposure and outcome variables are conditionally independent across units. These couplings can therefore be combined into a product coupling that preserves the observational and interventional score-vector marginals and their joint laws with the corresponding target potential outcome. Under this coupling, for y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

VIint​(y)=VI​(y), and Vjint=Vjobs,j∈𝒰Iex,\displaystyle V_{I}^{\mathrm{int}}(y)=V_{I}(y),\quad\text{ and }\quad V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}=V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\qquad j\in\mathcal{U}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}, (81)

almost surely. The conformal weights are also unchanged because the intervention does not alter the covariates.

Consequently, the unaffected units cancel from the difference between the two pp-values and

pI,yint−pI,yobs\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}-p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}} =∑j∈ℋIexWj[𝟙{Vjint≥VI(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VI(y)}]WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}}W_{j}\left[\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}\right]}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (82)

Note that for every j∈ℋIexj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}},

𝟙{Vjint≥VI(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VI(y)}≤𝟙{Vjobs<VI(y)},\displaystyle\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}\leq\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\}, (83)

and therefore,

pI,yint−pI,yobs≤∑j∈ℋIexWj𝟙{Vjobs<VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj≤∑j∈ℋIWj𝟙{Vjobs<VI(y)}WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj=ρI,y.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}-p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}\leq\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\}}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}=\rho_{I,y}. (84)

Hence,

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,yex≤pI,yobs+ρI,ya.s.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho^{\rm ex}_{I,y}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}\qquad\text{a.s.} (85)

Since the coupling does not depend on yy, this inequality holds simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. ∎

C.3 Coverage of IA-WCP

Use the joint coupling constructed in Lemma 3. It preserves the joint law of the interventional scores and target outcome and satisfies

YI​(1)=Y~II​(1),pI,YI​(1)int=pI,Y~II​(1)int\displaystyle Y_{I}(1)=\tilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1),\qquad p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}=p_{I,\tilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}} (86)

almost surely.

For each fixed II, the events Aℐ1,IA_{\mathcal{I}_{1},I}, indexed by the possible treated sets ℐ1⊆{1,…,N}∖{I}\mathcal{I}_{1}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus\{I\}, partition the event {TI=0}\{T_{I}=0\}. Averaging (71) over these events and over the randomly selected index II, and using the target equality under the coupling, yields

Pr⁡[pI,YI​(1)int≤α|TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\middle|T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (87)

By Lemma 3, under the same coupling, almost surely and simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,y.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}. (88)

Since overlap ensures pI,yobs>0p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>0, rejection is impossible when ρI,y≥α\rho_{I,y}\geq\alpha. Otherwise, rejection implies pI,yobs+ρI,y≤αp_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}\leq\alpha. Therefore,

{pI,yobs≤(α−ρI,y)+}⊆{pI,yint≤α}.\displaystyle\left\{p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq(\alpha-\rho_{I,y})_{+}\right\}\subseteq\left\{p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\right\}. (89)

Applying this inclusion at y=YI​(1)y=Y_{I}(1) gives

Pr⁡[pI,YI​(1)obs≤(α−ρI,YI​(1))+|TI=0]\displaystyle\Pr\left[p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq(\alpha-\rho_{I,Y_{I}(1)})_{+}\middle|T_{I}=0\right] ≤Pr⁡[pI,YI​(1)int≤α|TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\leq\Pr\left[p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\middle|T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (90)

By definition of the IA-WCP prediction set in (25),

YI(1)∉ΓIIA−WCP⟺pI,YI​(1)obs≤(α−ρI,YI​(1))+.\displaystyle Y_{I}(1)\notin\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq(\alpha-\rho_{I,Y_{I}(1)})_{+}. (91)

Hence,

Pr⁡[YI​(1)∉ΓIIA−WCP|TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\notin\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\middle|T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (92)

This proves Theorem 1.

We give an example in which the IA-WCP set in (25) is tight in the sense that it achieves the same marginal coverage as the ideal WCP set in (29). Fix a population size N≥2N\geq 2 and set the miscoverage level to α=αN=1/N\alpha=\alpha_{N}=1/N. For a constant propensity π∈(0,1)\pi\in(0,1), covariates and treatments are generated as

Xi\displaystyle X_{i} ∼iid​Unif⁡(0,1),\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}(0,1), Ti\displaystyle T_{i} ∼iid​Bernoulli⁡(π),i∈{1,…,N}.\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi),\qquad i\in\{1,\dots,N\}. (93)

𝒩i(X1:N)={ℓ≠i:Xℓ<Xi}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{\ell\neq i:X_{\ell}<X_{i}\}. (94)

We consider an exposure mechanism in which the exposure EiE_{i} of unit ii is determined by the number of control units in this neighborhood, i.e.,

Ei\displaystyle E_{i} =∑ℓ≠i(1−Tℓ)𝟙{Xℓ<Xi}.\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell\neq i}(1-T_{\ell})\mathds{1}\{X_{\ell}<X_{i}\}. (95)

Yi​(1)\displaystyle Y_{i}(1) ={Xi,Ei=0,−1,Ei≥1,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}X_{i},&E_{i}=0,\\ -1,&E_{i}\geq 1,\end{cases} Yi​(0)\displaystyle Y_{i}(0) =0.\displaystyle=0. (96)

The deterministic exposure and outcome kernels also satisfy the conditional-independence requirements in Assumptions 3 and 4. Take 𝒴=[−1,1]\mathcal{Y}=[-1,1] and use the nonconformity score

S⁡(x,e,y)=y.\displaystyle S(x,e,y)=y. (97)

We use the ideal WCP set Γ~IWCP\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\mathrm{WCP}} in (29) and the IA-WCP set ΓIIA−WCP\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}} in (25), both evaluated at miscoverage level αN\alpha_{N}.

Under the construction in (93)–(97), conditionally on TI=0T_{I}=0, the adjusted and interventional prediction sets have the same marginal coverage,

Pr⁡[YI​(1)∈Γ~IWCP∣TI=0]=Pr⁡[YI​(1)∈ΓIIA−WCP∣TI=0]=1−πN−1N≥1−αN.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\in\tilde{\Gamma}_{I}^{\mathrm{WCP}}\mid T_{I}=0\right]=\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\in\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\mid T_{I}=0\right]=1-\frac{\pi^{N-1}}{N}\geq 1-\alpha_{N}. (98)

ℋI=ℋIex={j≠I:Xj>XI}.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{I}=\mathcal{H}_{I}^{\mathrm{ex}}=\{j\neq I:X_{j}>X_{I}\}. (102)

pI,YI​(1)obs=1N,ρI,YI​(1)=HN,pI,YI​(1)int=H+1N.\displaystyle p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{1}{N},\qquad\rho_{I,Y_{I}(1)}=\frac{H}{N},\qquad p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{H+1}{N}. (103)
