Appendix E Transductive IA-WCP+

As mentioned in Section 3.2, IA-WCP+ leverages bounds on intervention-induced changes in the affected calibration scores to produce a sharper correction than the worst-case correction of IA-WCP. In this section, we formalize the stability condition under which the refined correction ρI,y+\rho_{I,y}^{+} introduced in (33) preserves marginal coverage. Throughout, we use the notation of Section 3, condition on TI=0T_{I}=0, and impose the following stability assumption on the affected calibration scores.

Assumption 6.

For every affected calibration unit j∈ℋIj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}, there exists a finite, nonnegative, observable margin ΔjI\Delta_{j}^{I} that is a measurable function of (X1:N,T1:N,I,Ej,Yj(1))(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I,E_{j},Y_{j}(1)), but does not depend on the random exposures or outcomes of other units, such that for every t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R},

Pr[Vjint>t∣X1:N,T1:N,I]≤Pr[Vjobs+ΔjI>t∣X1:N,T1:N,I].\displaystyle\Pr\left[V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}>t\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I\right]\leq\Pr\left[V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\Delta_{j}^{I}>t\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I\right]. (106)

Assumption 6 states that, conditionally on the covariates, treatment assignments, and target index, the interventional score of each affected unit is stochastically dominated by its observational score shifted upward by ΔjI\Delta_{j}^{I}. As shown in Section E.1, sufficient conditions for this assumption include Lipschitz continuity of the nonconformity score and almost-sure bounds on the intervention-induced changes in exposures and potential outcomes.

Using margins satisfying (106) in the correction factor (33), IA-WCP+ defines the prediction set as

ΓIIA−WCP+={y∈𝒴:pI,yobs>(α−ρI,y+)+},α∈(0,1).\displaystyle\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}+}=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>(\alpha-\rho_{I,y}^{+})_{+}\right\},\qquad\alpha\in(0,1). (107)

Since 0≤ρI,y+≤ρI,y0\leq\rho_{I,y}^{+}\leq\rho_{I,y} for every yy, comparing the acceptance thresholds in (107) and (25) gives

ΓIIA−WCP+⊆ΓIIA−WCP.\displaystyle\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}+}\subseteq\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}. (108)

Thus, IA-WCP+ returns a prediction set no larger than IA-WCP for the same observational sample. Under the assumptions of the following lemma, pI,yobs+ρI,y+p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}^{+} bounds the interventional pp-value from above under a suitable coupling.

Lemma 4.

Under Assumptions 3, 4, and 6, conditionally on TI=0T_{I}=0, the observational and interventional conformal pp-values admit a coupling such that, simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,y+a.s.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}^{+}\qquad\text{a.s.} (109)
Proof.

Work conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N,I)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I) with TI=0T_{I}=0, and write 𝒰I=ℐ1∖ℋI\mathcal{U}_{I}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{H}_{I}. As in Lemma 3, the observational and interventional scores can be coupled so that

VIint​(y)=VI​(y), and Vjobs=Vjinta.s. for every ​j∈𝒰I.\displaystyle V_{I}^{\mathrm{int}}(y)=V_{I}(y),\quad\text{ and }\quad V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}=V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\qquad\text{a.s. for every }j\in\mathcal{U}_{I}. (110)

For every j∈ℋIj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}, Assumption 6 and the coupling characterization of stochastic order (Strassen, 1965) imply the existence of a coupling, preserving the conditional joint law of (Vjobs,ΔjI)(V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\Delta_{j}^{I}), such that

Vjint≤Vjobs+ΔjIa.s.\displaystyle V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\Delta_{j}^{I}\qquad\text{a.s.} (111)

Since, conditional on (X1:N,T1:N,I)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I), each ΔjI\Delta_{j}^{I} may depend only on (Ej,Yj​(1))(E_{j},Y_{j}(1)) and not on the exposures or outcomes of other units, the pair (Vjobs,ΔjI)(V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\Delta_{j}^{I}) is a function only of the random variables (Ej,Yj​(1))(E_{j},Y_{j}(1)). From Assumptions 3 and 4 it then follows that the pairs (Vjobs,ΔjI)(V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\Delta_{j}^{I}) are conditionally independent across units. The unit couplings can therefore be combined into a product coupling under which (111) holds simultaneously for every j∈ℋIj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}.

The interventional scores are conditionally independent for the same reason. The product coupling therefore preserves both score-vector marginals. We also retain the identical target coupling (E~II,Y~II​(1))=(EI,YI​(1))(\tilde{E}_{I}^{I},\tilde{Y}_{I}^{I}(1))=(E_{I},Y_{I}(1)) from Lemma 3, preserving the joint laws with the target potential outcome.

For every j∈ℋIj\in\mathcal{H}_{I}, (111) implies

𝟙{Vjint≥VI(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VI(y)}≤𝟙{VI(y)−ΔjI≤Vjobs<VI(y)}.\displaystyle\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}\leq\mathds{1}\left\{V_{I}(y)-\Delta_{j}^{I}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\right\}. (112)

In fact, the left-hand side can be positive only if

Vjobs<VI​(y)≤Vjint≤Vjobs+ΔjI.\displaystyle V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{I}(y)\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\Delta_{j}^{I}. (113)

Since the unaffected scores coincide under the coupling,

pI,yint−pI,yobs\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}-p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}} =∑j∈ℋIWj[𝟙{Vjint≥VI(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VI(y)}]WI+∑j∈ℐ1Wj≤ρI,y+.\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{I}}W_{j}\left[\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{I}(y)\}\right]}{W_{I}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}\leq\rho_{I,y}^{+}. (114)

Therefore,

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,y+a.s.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}^{+}\qquad\text{a.s.} (115)

Since the coupling does not depend on yy, the inequality holds simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. ∎

It follows that IA-WCP+ preserves marginal coverage, as formalized in the following theorem.

Theorem 2.

Under Assumptions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, the prediction set in (107) satisfies

Pr⁡[YI​(1)∉ΓIIA−WCP+∣TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{I}(1)\notin\Gamma_{I}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}+}\mid T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (116)
Proof.

The interventional superuniformity established in (87) gives

Pr⁡[pI,YI​(1)int≤α∣TI=0]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[p_{I,Y_{I}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\mid T_{I}=0\right]\leq\alpha. (117)

By Lemma 4,

pI,yint≤pI,yobs+ρI,y+.\displaystyle p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho^{+}_{I,y}. (118)

Since overlap ensures pI,yobs>0p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>0, rejection is impossible when ρI,y+≥α\rho_{I,y}^{+}\geq\alpha. Otherwise, rejection implies pI,yobs+ρI,y+≤αp_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{I,y}^{+}\leq\alpha. Thus, under this coupling,

{pI,yobs≤(α−ρI,y+)+}⊆{pI,yint≤α}.\displaystyle\left\{p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq\left(\alpha-\rho^{+}_{I,y}\right)_{+}\right\}\subseteq\left\{p_{I,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\right\}. (119)

The coupling preserves the joint law with YI​(1)Y_{I}(1) and holds simultaneously for every yy. Evaluating at y=YI​(1)y=Y_{I}(1) therefore proves the claim. ∎

E.1 Sufficient conditions for score stability

Let dℰ:ℰ×ℰ→[0,∞)d_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{E}\to[0,\infty) be a metric on the exposure space ℰ\mathcal{E}. Conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N,I)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},I), suppose that the observational and interventional exposures and outcomes of every affected unit j∈ℋIj\in\mathcal{H}_{I} admit a coupling with the correct conditional marginals satisfying

dℰ​(Ej,E~jI)\displaystyle d_{\mathcal{E}}(E_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}^{I}) ≤ΔE,jI,\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{E,j}^{I}, (120)
|Yj​(1)−Y~jI​(1)|\displaystyle\left|Y_{j}(1)-\tilde{Y}_{j}^{I}(1)\right| ≤ΔY,jI\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{Y,j}^{I} (121)

almost surely, where the two bounds are finite, nonnegative, and observable, with the same local dependence allowed for ΔjI\Delta_{j}^{I} in Assumption 6. Suppose also that the nonconformity score satisfies, for finite constants LE,LY≥0L_{E},L_{Y}\geq 0,

|S⁡(x,e,y)−S⁡(x,e′,y′)|≤LE​dℰ​(e,e′)+LY​|y−y′|.\displaystyle\left|S(x,e,y)-S(x,e^{\prime},y^{\prime})\right|\leq L_{E}d_{\mathcal{E}}(e,e^{\prime})+L_{Y}|y-y^{\prime}|. (122)

Then

|Vjint−Vjobs|≤LE​ΔE,jI+LY​ΔY,jI\displaystyle\left|V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}-V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right|\leq L_{E}\Delta_{E,j}^{I}+L_{Y}\Delta_{Y,j}^{I} (123)

almost surely. Hence, Assumption 6 holds with

ΔjI=LE​ΔE,jI+LY​ΔY,jI.\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{I}=L_{E}\Delta_{E,j}^{I}+L_{Y}\Delta_{Y,j}^{I}. (124)

If the score does not depend on the exposure, the same conclusion holds with

ΔjI=LY​ΔY,jI.\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{I}=L_{Y}\Delta_{Y,j}^{I}. (125)

Appendix F Inductive Interference-Adjusted Weighted Conformal Prediction

In this section, we consider the inductive setting described in Section 2.1.2. Given data 𝒟\mathcal{D} from a network of N−1N-1 units, we construct a prediction set for the ITE of a new unit with covariates XN∼PXX_{N}\sim P_{X} after it is embedded in the network. We outline how the reasoning developed for the transductive setting in Section 3 extends to this case. In what follows, we construct a prediction set for the treated potential outcome YN​(1)Y_{N}(1).

As in the transductive setting, a direct application of WCP to the treated calibration units ℐ1={j∈{1,…,N−1}:Tj=1}\mathcal{I}_{1}=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}:T_{j}=1\} does not generally guarantee coverage for YN​(1)Y_{N}(1). In fact, inverse-propensity weighting with weights

Wj=1π⁡(Xj), for ​j∈ℐ1∪{N},\displaystyle W_{j}=\frac{1}{\pi(X_{j})},\quad\text{ for }j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{N\}, (126)

accounts for the difference between the covariate distributions of the treated calibration units and the new unit. However, the calibration exposures and outcomes are generated in the original network of N−1N-1 units, whereas the test exposure ENE_{N} and outcome YN​(1)Y_{N}(1) are generated in the augmented network of NN units. Consequently, the calibration scores Vjobs=S⁡(Xj,Ej,Yj​(1))V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}=S(X_{j},E_{j},Y_{j}(1)), for j∈ℐ1j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, and the test score VN​(YN​(1))V_{N}(Y_{N}(1)) need not be weighted exchangeable. Thus, the observational conformal pp-value

pN,yobs=WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj𝟙{Vjobs≥VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}} (127)

need not be valid.

To correct this procedure, we follow the same interventional reasoning as in the transductive setting. Consider adding unit NN with treatment TN=1T_{N}=1 and regenerating the calibration exposures and potential outcomes according to the model in the augmented network. Under this intervention, calibration and test units become weighted exchangeable with weights WjW_{j}. Replacing the observational calibration scores in pN,yobsp_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}} with their interventional counterparts yields an ideal WCP procedure with the desired marginal coverage guarantee.

To relate the ideal but unobservable procedure to the observational one, IA-WCP defines the treated calibration units whose neighborhoods change when unit NN is added to the network

ℋN={j∈ℐ1:𝒩j(X1:N−1)≠𝒩j(X1:N)},\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{N}=\left\{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}:\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N-1})\neq\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N})\right\}, (128)

and evaluates the correction factor

ρN,y=∑j∈ℋNWj𝟙{Vjobs<VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle\rho_{N,y}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{N}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (129)

The factor (129) accounts for the discrepancy between the observational and interventional conformal pp-values and it is used to define the IA-WCP prediction set

ΓNIA−WCP={y∈𝒴:pN,yobs>(α−ρN,y)+}.\displaystyle\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>(\alpha-\rho_{N,y})_{+}\right\}. (130)

A suitable coupling of the observational and interventional scores ensures that the IA-WCP set contains the ideal WCP set, yielding the following coverage guarantee.

Theorem 3 (Inductive IA-WCP coverage).

Under Assumptions 1–5, the IA-WCP set ΓNIA−WCP\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}} in (130) satisfies the inequality

Pr[YN(1)∈ΓNIA−WCP]≥1−α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{N}(1)\in\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\right]\geq 1-\alpha. (131)
Proof.

See Appendix G. ∎

For YN​(0)Y_{N}(0), the corresponding prediction set is obtained using the control units and weights 1/(1−π⁡(Xj))1/(1-\pi(X_{j})). To distinguish the two constructions, we now make the target treatment explicit in the notation. Let ΓNt,IA−WCP\Gamma_{N}^{t,\mathrm{IA-WCP}} denote the prediction set for YN​(t)Y_{N}(t) constructed at miscoverage level αt\alpha_{t}. Choosing α1+α0=α\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{0}=\alpha, the ITE prediction set is defined as

ΓNITE={y1−y0:y1∈ΓN1,IA−WCP,y0∈ΓN0,IA−WCP},\displaystyle\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{ITE}}=\left\{y_{1}-y_{0}:y_{1}\in\Gamma_{N}^{1,\mathrm{IA-WCP}},y_{0}\in\Gamma_{N}^{0,\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\right\}, (132)

and it satisfies (20) by the union bound.

F.1 Inductive IA-WCP+

As in the transductive setting, the correction can be sharpened when the intervention-induced increase in each affected calibration score is stochastically bounded.

Assumption 7.

For every affected calibration unit j∈ℋNj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}, there exists a finite, nonnegative, observable margin ΔjN\Delta_{j}^{N} that is a measurable function of (X1:N,T1:N,Ej,Yj(1))(X_{1:N},T_{1:N},E_{j},Y_{j}(1)), but does not depend on the random exposures or outcomes of other units, such that for every t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R},

Pr[Vjint>t∣X1:N,T1:N]≤Pr[Vjobs+ΔjN>t∣X1:N,T1:N].\displaystyle\Pr\left[V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}>t\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N}\right]\leq\Pr\left[V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\Delta_{j}^{N}>t\mid X_{1:N},T_{1:N}\right]. (133)

Assumption 7 states that, conditionally on the augmented covariate and treatment vectors, the interventional score of each affected calibration unit is stochastically dominated by its observational score shifted upward by ΔjN\Delta_{j}^{N}. Using the stability margins in (133), IA-WCP+ defines the refined correction factor

ρN,y+=∑j∈ℋNWj𝟙{VN(y)−ΔjN≤Vjobs<VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle\rho_{N,y}^{+}=\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{N}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\left\{V_{N}(y)-\Delta_{j}^{N}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\right\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (134)

Under Assumption 7, the observational and interventional score vectors admit a coupling with the correct conditional marginals such that, simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pN,yint≤pN,yobs+ρN,y+a.s.\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{N,y}^{+}\qquad\text{a.s.} (135)

The correction ρN,y+\rho_{N,y}^{+} counts only the conformal weight of affected calibration units whose observational scores lie within a margin ΔjN\Delta_{j}^{N} below the test score.

Under this coupling, every candidate accepted by the ideal interventional procedure is also accepted by the adjusted observational procedure. This motivates the IA-WCP+ prediction set

ΓNIA−WCP+={y∈𝒴:pN,yobs>(α−ρN,y+)+}.\displaystyle\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP+}}=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>(\alpha-\rho_{N,y}^{+})_{+}\right\}. (136)

Because ρN,y+≤ρN,y\rho_{N,y}^{+}\leq\rho_{N,y}, the IA-WCP+ prediction set ΓNIA−WCP+\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP+}} is contained in the IA-WCP prediction set ΓN1,IA−WCP\Gamma_{N}^{1,\mathrm{IA-WCP}} in (130).

Theorem 4.

Under Assumptions 1–5 and 7, the IA-WCP+ prediction set in (136) satisfies

Pr[YN(1)∉ΓNIA−WCP+]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{N}(1)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP+}}\right]\leq\alpha. (137)
Proof.

See Appendix G.4. ∎

Appendix G Proofs of Inductive IA-WCP and Inductive IA-WCP+ Validity

In this section, we provide the proofs of Theorem 3 and Theorem 4. Throughout, the observational network contains N−1N-1 units and the new unit is indexed by NN, as in the main text. Following the same template as the transductive case, we first establish the validity of ideal WCP in the augmented network, then compare its scores with the observational scores through a coupling and establish the validity of IA-WCP. In Appendix G.4 we show that the same reasoning applies to IA-WCP+ under the score stability condition stated in Assumption 7.

G.1 Validity of the ideal WCP procedure

We consider the case in which the test unit is embedded into the observed network with treatment TN=1T_{N}=1 and we wish to estimate its potential outcome YN​(1)Y_{N}(1). Define the augmented covariate and treatment vectors

X1:N=(X1,…,XN−1,XN),T1:N=(T1,…,TN−1,1),\displaystyle X_{1:N}=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{N-1},X_{N}),\qquad T_{1:N}=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{N-1},1), (138)

where XN∼PXX_{N}\sim P_{X} is independent of the observed covariates X1:N−1X_{1:N-1} and treatments T1:N−1T_{1:N-1}. For each treated calibration unit j∈ℐ1j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, let E~j\tilde{E}_{j} denote the exposure of unit jj in the augmented network, and let Y~j​(1)\tilde{Y}_{j}(1) denote the corresponding treated potential outcome. Thus,

E~j∣(X1:N,T1:N)∼PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T1:N)),\displaystyle\tilde{E}_{j}\mid(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right), (139)

and

Y~j(1)∣Xj,E~j∼PY⁡(1)|X,E(⋅∣Xj,E~j).\displaystyle\tilde{Y}_{j}(1)\mid X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}\sim P_{Y(1)\mid X,E}(\cdot\mid X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j}). (140)

For the test unit, let

EN∣(X1:N,T1:N)∼PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣XN,ℒN(X1:N,T1:N)),\displaystyle E_{N}\mid(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\sim P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{N},\mathcal{L}_{N}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right), (141)

and

YN(1)∣XN,EN∼PY⁡(1)|X,E(⋅∣XN,EN).\displaystyle Y_{N}(1)\mid X_{N},E_{N}\sim P_{Y(1)\mid X,E}(\cdot\mid X_{N},E_{N}). (142)

We define the interventional nonconformity scores Vjint=S⁡(Xj,E~j,Y~j​(1))V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}=S(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j},\tilde{Y}_{j}(1)) and the triples

Z~j=(Xj,E~j,Y~j​(1)),j∈ℐ1,\displaystyle\tilde{Z}_{j}=(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j},\tilde{Y}_{j}(1)),\qquad j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, (143)

and

ZN=(XN,EN,YN​(1)).\displaystyle Z_{N}=(X_{N},E_{N},Y_{N}(1)). (144)

We first establish the weighted exchangeability of the augmented interventional sample.

Lemma 5 (Inductive weighted exchangeability).

Under Assumptions 1, 3, 4, and 2, the joint density of

((Z~j)j∈ℐ1,ZN),\displaystyle\bigl((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}},Z_{N}\bigr), (145)

conditional on the realized treated set ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1}, admits the decomposition

p⁡((Z~j)j∈ℐ1,ZN∣ℐ1)=c​w​(XN)​g​((Z~j)j∈ℐ1,ZN),\displaystyle p\left((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}},Z_{N}\mid\mathcal{I}_{1}\right)=cw(X_{N})g\left((\tilde{Z}_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}},Z_{N}\right), (146)

where c>0c>0 is a normalizing constant,

w⁡(x)=1π⁡(x),\displaystyle w(x)=\frac{1}{\pi(x)}, (147)

and g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) is invariant under permutations of its arguments.

Proof.

Conditionally on the event defining the treated calibration set ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1}, the covariates of treated calibration units have density proportional to π⁡(x)​pX​(x)\pi(x)p_{X}(x). In contrast, the test-unit covariate has density pX​(x)p_{X}(x). Since

pX​(XN)=w⁡(XN)​π​(XN)​pX​(XN),w⁡(x)=1π⁡(x),\displaystyle p_{X}(X_{N})=w(X_{N})\pi(X_{N})p_{X}(X_{N}),\qquad w(x)=\frac{1}{\pi(x)}, (148)

the covariate density of the augmented sample can be written, up to a normalizing constant, as

w⁡(XN)​∏j∈ℐ1π⁡(Xj)​pX​(Xj)​π​(XN)​pX​(XN).\displaystyle w(X_{N})\prod_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}\pi(X_{j})p_{X}(X_{j})\pi(X_{N})p_{X}(X_{N}). (149)

After extracting the factor w⁡(XN)w(X_{N}), the remaining covariate density is symmetric in the augmented covariates {Xj:j∈ℐ1}∪{XN}\{X_{j}:j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}\}\cup\{X_{N}\}.

Under the augmented treatment vector T1:NT_{1:N}, all units in ℐ1∪{N}\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{N\} have treatment equal to one. By Assumption 3, the exposure variables are conditionally independent given the augmented covariates and treatments. By Assumption 4, the corresponding treated potential outcomes are conditionally independent given their covariates and exposures, with common conditional distribution PY⁡(1)|X,EP_{Y(1)\mid X,E}.

It remains to check the invariance of the remaining factor. Since all units in the augmented set ℐ1∪{N}\mathcal{I}_{1}\cup\{N\} have treatment equal to one, permuting these units only relabels their positions. By the permutation equivariance of the neighborhood rule in Assumption 2 and the ordering invariance of the common exposure kernel, the joint exposure distribution is unchanged under a simultaneous permutation of the triples

(Xj,E~j,Y~j​(1)),j∈ℐ1,\displaystyle(X_{j},\tilde{E}_{j},\tilde{Y}_{j}(1)),\qquad j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}, (150)

and the test triple (XN,EN,YN​(1))(X_{N},E_{N},Y_{N}(1)). Covariates and variables of the control units are integrated out; their contribution is unchanged by such a relabeling. Hence the remaining factor g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) is invariant under permutations of the augmented sample, proving the claim. ∎

By Lemma 5, the augmented interventional sample is weighted exchangeable with weights w⁡(x)=1/π⁡(x)w(x)=1/\pi(x). Therefore, the standard weighted conformal validity argument (Lei and Candès, 2021) implies that the ideal interventional conformal pp-value

pN,yint=WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj𝟙{Vjint≥VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}=\frac{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}} (151)

is valid and the ideal prediction set

Γ~NWCP={y∈𝒴:pN,yint>α}\displaystyle\tilde{\Gamma}_{N}^{\mathrm{WCP}}=\{y\in\mathcal{Y}:p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}>\alpha\} (152)

satisfies

Pr[YN(1)∈Γ~NWCP]≥1−α.\displaystyle\Pr[Y_{N}(1)\in\tilde{\Gamma}_{N}^{\mathrm{WCP}}]\geq 1-\alpha. (153)

G.2 Coupling comparison

Recall the definition of the units affected by the addition of unit NN to the network,

ℋN={j∈ℐ1:𝒩j(X1:N−1)≠𝒩j(X1:N)},\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{N}=\{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}:\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N-1})\neq\mathcal{N}_{j}(X_{1:N})\}, (154)

and write 𝒰N=ℐ1∖ℋN\mathcal{U}_{N}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{H}_{N}. For the proof, we consider the tighter exposure-law affected set

ℋNex={j∈ℐ1:\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}=\Bigl\{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}: PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N−1,T1:N−1))≠PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T1:N))},\displaystyle P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N-1},T_{1:N-1})\right)\neq P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})\right)\Bigr\}, (155)

and let 𝒰Nex=ℐ1∖ℋNex\mathcal{U}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}=\mathcal{I}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}. Since equal neighborhoods give equal local configurations before and after augmentation, ℋNex⊆ℋN.\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{N}. The tighter set ℋNex\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}} is used to construct the coupling, after which the index set of the nonnegative correction sum is enlarged from ℋNex\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}} to ℋN\mathcal{H}_{N}.

Lemma 6.

Under Assumptions 3 and 4, define the observational conformal pp-value by

pN,yobs=WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj𝟙{Vjobs≥VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (156)

Then this pp-value and the interventional conformal pp-value in (151) admit a coupling such that, simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pN,yint≤pN,yobs+ρN,ya.s.,\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{N,y}\qquad\text{a.s.}, (157)

where ρN,y\rho_{N,y} is defined in (129).

Proof.

We construct the coupling conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}). For every j∈𝒰Nexj\in\mathcal{U}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}, the definition of 𝒰Nex\mathcal{U}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}} gives

PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N−1,T1:N−1))=PE|X,ℒ(⋅∣Xj,ℒj(X1:N,T1:N)).\displaystyle P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid{X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N-1},T_{1:N-1})}\right)=P_{E\mid X,\mathcal{L}}\left(\cdot\mid{X_{j},\mathcal{L}_{j}(X_{1:N},T_{1:N})}\right). (158)

Thus, for each j∈𝒰Nexj\in\mathcal{U}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}, the observational and interventional exposures may be coupled so that

Ej=E~ja.s.\displaystyle E_{j}=\tilde{E}_{j}\qquad\text{a.s.} (159)

Conditional on these coupled exposures, the corresponding treated potential outcomes have the same conditional distribution PY⁡(1)|X,EP_{Y(1)\mid X,E} and may therefore be coupled so that

Yj​(1)=Y~j​(1)a.s.\displaystyle Y_{j}(1)=\tilde{Y}_{j}(1)\qquad\text{a.s.} (160)

For every j∈ℋNexj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}, choose any coupling with the correct observational and interventional marginals.

By Assumptions 3 and 4, the unit-specific exposure and outcome variables are conditionally independent across units. These couplings can therefore be combined into a product coupling that preserves the observational and interventional score-vector marginals. Under this coupling,

Vjobs=Vjinta.s. for every ​j∈𝒰Nex.\displaystyle V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}=V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\qquad\text{a.s. for every }{j\in\mathcal{U}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}}. (161)

The test exposure and outcome have the same joint law with the augmented covariates and treatments in both constructions, and are coupled identically. The two pp-values therefore use the same target score VN​(y)V_{N}(y) and the same weights, since the weights depend only on the covariates. Consequently,

pN,yint−pN,yobs\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}-p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}} =∑j∈ℋNexWj[𝟙{Vjint≥VN(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VN(y)}]WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj.\displaystyle=\frac{{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}}}W_{j}\left[\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}\right]}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}. (162)

For every j∈ℋNexj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}},

𝟙{Vjint≥VN(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VN(y)}≤𝟙{Vjobs<VN(y)}.\displaystyle\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}\leq\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\}. (163)

Therefore,

pN,yint−pN,yobs≤∑j∈ℋNexWj𝟙{Vjobs<VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}-p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{N}^{\mathrm{ex}}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}} ≤∑j∈ℋNWj𝟙{Vjobs<VN(y)}WN+∑j∈ℐ1Wj=ρN,y.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{H}_{N}}W_{j}\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\}}{W_{N}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{1}}W_{j}}=\rho_{N,y}. (164)

Hence,

pN,yint≤pN,yobs+ρN,ya.s.\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{N,y}\qquad\text{a.s.} (165)

Since the coupling does not depend on yy, this inequality holds simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. ∎

G.3 Proof of Theorem 3

By Lemma 6, there is a coupling preserving the observational and interventional marginals such that pN,yint≤pN,yobs+ρN,yp_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{N,y} simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. If ρN,y<α\rho_{N,y}<\alpha, then pN,yint>αp_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}>\alpha implies pN,yobs>α−ρN,yp_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>\alpha-\rho_{N,y}. If ρN,y≥α\rho_{N,y}\geq\alpha, the IA-WCP acceptance threshold is zero, and pN,yobs>0p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>0 because WN>0W_{N}>0. Hence,

Γ~NWCP⊆ΓNIA−WCPa.s.\displaystyle\tilde{\Gamma}_{N}^{\mathrm{WCP}}\subseteq\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}\qquad\text{a.s.} (166)

Evaluating this inclusion at the shared target outcome and using the validity of the interventional pp-value gives

Pr[YN(1)∉ΓNIA−WCP]≤Pr[pN,YN​(1)int≤α]≤α,\displaystyle\Pr[Y_{N}(1)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP}}]\leq\Pr[p_{N,Y_{N}(1)}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha]\leq\alpha, (167)

which proves Theorem 3.

For the control potential outcome, fix the target treatment at zero, use the control calibration units and weights 1/(1−π⁡(Xj))1/(1-\pi(X_{j})), and repeat the argument. Write ΓNt,IA−WCP\Gamma_{N}^{t,\mathrm{IA-WCP}} for the set targeting YN​(t)Y_{N}(t) at miscoverage level αt\alpha_{t}. Since the neighborhood excludes the unit itself, the target exposure law is unchanged by its own treatment; both potential-outcome guarantees therefore apply to the common target exposure in the ITE definition. If both potential outcomes belong to their respective prediction sets, their difference belongs to ΓNITE\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{ITE}}. Thus,

Pr[YN(1)−YN(0)∉ΓNITE]\displaystyle\Pr[Y_{N}(1)-Y_{N}(0)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{ITE}}] ≤Pr[YN(1)∉ΓN1,IA−WCP]+Pr[YN(0)∉ΓN0,IA−WCP]≤α1+α0=α.\displaystyle\leq\Pr[Y_{N}(1)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{1,\mathrm{IA-WCP}}]+\Pr[Y_{N}(0)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{0,\mathrm{IA-WCP}}]\leq\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{0}=\alpha. (168)

G.4 Proof of Theorem 4

For every j∈𝒰Nj\in\mathcal{U}_{N}, the coupling in the proof of Lemma 6 gives

Vjint=Vjobsa.s.\displaystyle V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}=V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\qquad\text{a.s.} (169)

For every j∈ℋNj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}, Assumption 7 establishes the required conditional stochastic ordering. By the coupling characterization of stochastic order (Strassen, 1965), applied conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}), there exists a coupling of VjintV_{j}^{\mathrm{int}} and (Vjobs,ΔjN)(V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\Delta_{j}^{N}) with the correct conditional marginals such that

Vjint≤Vjobs+ΔjNa.s.\displaystyle V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\Delta_{j}^{N}\qquad\text{a.s.} (170)

Conditionally on (X1:N,T1:N)(X_{1:N},T_{1:N}), each pair (Vjobs,ΔjN)(V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}},\Delta_{j}^{N}) depends only on (Ej,Yj​(1))(E_{j},Y_{j}(1)). Assumptions 3 and 4 therefore imply that these pairs are conditionally independent across units. The interventional scores are conditionally independent for the same reason. Hence, the coordinatewise couplings can be combined into a product coupling under which (170) holds simultaneously for every j∈ℋNj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}, while preserving the observational and interventional score-vector marginals.

For every j∈ℋNj\in\mathcal{H}_{N}, (170) implies

𝟙{Vjint≥VN(y)}−𝟙{Vjobs≥VN(y)}≤𝟙{VN(y)−ΔjN≤Vjobs<VN(y)}.\displaystyle\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{int}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}-\mathds{1}\{V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}\geq V_{N}(y)\}\leq\mathds{1}\left\{V_{N}(y)-\Delta_{j}^{N}\leq V_{j}^{\mathrm{obs}}<V_{N}(y)\right\}. (171)

The target exposure and outcome are coupled identically, as in Lemma 6. Since the unaffected scores coincide under the coupling, the interventional and observational pp-values satisfy, simultaneously for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y},

pN,yint≤pN,yobs+ρN,y+a.s.\displaystyle p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}+\rho_{N,y}^{+}\qquad\text{a.s.} (172)

Because pN,yobs>0p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}>0, the same threshold argument used in Appendix G.3 gives

{pN,yobs≤(α−ρN,y+)+}⊆{pN,yint≤α}.\displaystyle\left\{p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{obs}}\leq(\alpha-\rho_{N,y}^{+})_{+}\right\}\subseteq\left\{p_{N,y}^{\mathrm{int}}\leq\alpha\right\}. (173)

Evaluating this inclusion at y=YN​(1)y=Y_{N}(1) yields

Pr[YN(1)∉ΓNIA−WCP+]≤α.\displaystyle\Pr\left[Y_{N}(1)\notin\Gamma_{N}^{\mathrm{IA-WCP+}}\right]\leq\alpha. (174)

Appendix H Additional Experiments

H.1 Traffic Slicing

In this section, we evaluate the proposed methods in a wireless traffic-slicing problem (Foukas et al., 2017; Bao et al., 2017). We consider a wireless-network setting in which a finite amount of radio resources is allocated among multiple users. The users are organized into traffic slices representing services with similar requirements, such as latency-sensitive, high-throughput, or best-effort traffic. Each slice is assigned a resource pool that must be shared among its scheduled users. Resource allocation therefore induces interference, since scheduling one user reduces the resources available to other scheduled users in the same slice. Consequently, a scheduled user’s outcome depends not only on its own channel and traffic characteristics, but also on the number of other scheduled users sharing the same resource pool (Foukas et al., 2017; Bao et al., 2017).

H.1.1 Setup

We consider a population of N=200N=200 devices sharing radio resources across NSN_{S} slices. Each device ii is characterized by a feature vector XiX_{i} that includes its channel-quality indicator, traffic characteristics, backlog information, and the slice ZiZ_{i} to which it is assigned. The binary treatment Ti∈{0,1}T_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether device ii is scheduled and granted radio resources (Ti=1T_{i}=1) or not (Ti=0T_{i}=0). Scheduling decisions are drawn independently according to

Ti|Xi∼Bernoulli⁡(π⁡(Xi)),\displaystyle T_{i}\mid X_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi(X_{i})), (175)

where the propensity score π⁡(Xi)\pi(X_{i}) is a function of the device covariates.

The neighborhood of device ii is the set of other devices assigned to the same slice,

𝒩i(X1:N)={j≠i:Zj=Zi},\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})=\{j\neq i:Z_{j}=Z_{i}\}, (176)

and the exposure of device ii corresponds to the number of users in this neighborhood that are scheduled,

Ei=∑j∈𝒩i(X1:N)Tj.\displaystyle E_{i}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}(X_{1:N})}T_{j}. (177)

Thus, the exposure EiE_{i} measures the same-slice contention experienced by device ii.

The potential outcome Yi​(t)Y_{i}(t) represents the throughput of device ii under the scheduling decision tt. If device ii is not scheduled, Ti=0T_{i}=0, it receives no radio resources and its throughput is zero, Yi​(0)=0Y_{i}(0)=0. When device ii is scheduled, its throughput depends on its channel quality and the amount of same-slice contention. Specifically, this is given by

Yi​(1)=min⁡{η⁡(Xi)​ξi(Ei+1)​NS,Rmax},\displaystyle Y_{i}(1)=\min\left\{\frac{\eta(X_{i})\xi_{i}}{(E_{i}+1)N_{S}},R_{\max}\right\}, (178)

where η⁡(Xi)\eta(X_{i}) is a spectral-efficiency term determined by the channel-quality indicator contained in XiX_{i}, and ξi\xi_{i} is a log-normal multiplicative noise variable normalized to have mean one. The factor NS−1N_{S}^{-1} represents the fraction of the total resources assigned to each slice, while the term (Ei+1)−1(E_{i}+1)^{-1} models equal resource sharing among all scheduled devices in the slice, including device ii. Consequently, greater exposure corresponds to stronger resource contention and lower achievable throughput. The throughput is capped at the maximum supported rate RmaxR_{\max}.

We use gradient-boosted quantile regression as the baseline predictor for the treated potential outcome. The predictor is trained on treated samples from five independently generated network realizations. The resulting lower and upper quantile estimates, q^α/2​(X)\hat{q}_{\alpha/2}(X) and q^1−α/2​(X)\hat{q}_{1-\alpha/2}(X), define the exposure-independent nonconformity score of each treated calibration device as

S⁡(Xi,Ei,Yi​(1))=max⁡{q^α/2​(Xi)−Yi​(1),Yi​(1)−q^1−α/2​(Xi)}.\displaystyle S(X_{i},E_{i},Y_{i}(1))=\max\left\{\hat{q}_{\alpha/2}(X_{i})-Y_{i}(1),Y_{i}(1)-\hat{q}_{1-\alpha/2}(X_{i})\right\}. (179)

H.1.2 Benchmarks

We consider transductive counterfactual estimation and implement the following methods: (a)(a) uncalibrated quantile-regression interval (QR) (Koenker and Bassett Jr, 1978), given by

ΓQR​(X)=[q^α/2​(X),q^1−α/2​(X)],\displaystyle\Gamma^{\rm QR}(X)=[\hat{q}_{\alpha/2}(X),\hat{q}_{1-\alpha/2}(X)], (180)

(b)(b) conventional WCP (Lei and Candès, 2021), (c)(c) ideal WCP, (d)(d) IA-WCP, and (e)(e) the stability-aware IA-WCP+. The last two methods are proposed in this work, while ideal WCP is the prediction set constructed from the interventional pp-value in (30). Ideal WCP is available in simulation because the data-generating mechanism allows us to recompute the interventional exposures and outcomes, and therefore serves as an oracle baseline. For IA-WCP+, intervening to schedule the target device II increases the exposure by one for every treated calibration device in the same slice, while leaving the other devices unaffected. Since the quantile-regression nonconformity score is 11-Lipschitz in the outcome, the score-stability condition in Assumption 6 is satisfied with

ΔjI=Yj​(1)Ej+2𝟙{Zj=ZI}.\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{I}=\frac{Y_{j}(1)}{E_{j}+2}\mathds{1}\{Z_{j}=Z_{I}\}. (181)

H.1.3 Results

Figure 7 reports the empirical coverage and normalized average prediction-set size at the target miscoverage level α=0.2\alpha=0.2, as the number of slices varies over NS∈{2,3,4,6,10,16,32}N_{S}\in\{2,3,4,6,10,16,32\}. For each network realization, both quantities are averaged over all unscheduled target devices. A smaller number of slices NSN_{S} corresponds to a larger average number of devices in each slice and stronger interference. By varying the number of slices NSN_{S} we evaluate the performance of the proposed methods under different interference regimes.

For every value of the number of slices NSN_{S}, the uncalibrated QR interval fails to attain the target coverage level 1−α=0.81-\alpha=0.8. WCP approaches nominal coverage when interference is weak, attaining coverage of approximately 0.810.81 at NS=32N_{S}=32. As the number of slices decreases and the level of interference increases, however, its coverage falls below the nominal level, reaching approximately 0.760.76 at NS=2N_{S}=2. In contrast, ideal WCP remains above the target coverage for all values of NSN_{S}. The coverage gap between WCP and ideal WCP illustrates the loss of validity caused by calibrating with observational scores.

Both proposed interference-adjusted methods maintain coverage above the target level for all values of NSN_{S}. IA-WCP uses a worst-case correction and therefore becomes highly conservative when a large fraction of the calibration weight is assigned to devices in the target slice. This conservativeness results in substantially larger prediction sets, particularly in the strongest-interference regimes. In contrast, IA-WCP+ mitigates this loss of efficiency by exploiting the device-specific stability margins in (181), and its coverage and prediction-set size remain close to those of ideal WCP.

H.2 Additional Synthetic Results

In this section, we consider the synthetic model introduced in Section 4 and present results that complement those in the main text. Specifically, we consider both transductive and inductive inference, additional target coverage levels, and experiments that vary the interference strength and outcome noise.

H.2.1 Interference Strength

Figure 8 reports the empirical coverage and normalized width of prediction sets returned by WCP, ideal WCP, the proposed IA-WCP, and IA-WCP+ in both the transductive and inductive settings as a function of the sigmoid parameter λ\lambda. The parameter λ\lambda controls the sharpness of the exposure-outcome mechanism in (36). In particular, when λ\lambda is close to zero, the exposure-outcome mechanism is flat and peer exposure has little effect on the treated outcome. As λ\lambda increases, the treated outcome changes rapidly depending on whether a majority of peers are treated.

For λ=0\lambda=0, WCP and ideal WCP coincide and attain the target coverage levels. In this regime, the observational calibration scores used by WCP are the same as the interventional calibration scores used by ideal WCP. However, as λ\lambda increases, the gap between WCP and ideal WCP becomes more visible, and WCP begins to fall below nominal coverage. This degradation is more pronounced in the transductive setting. IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ remain above the target coverage level across the range of values considered. WCP and ideal WCP remain relatively close in width, while IA-WCP becomes wider as the sigmoid parameter λ\lambda grows because it applies a worst-case correction for affected calibration units. In contrast, IA-WCP+ maintains a width close to that of ideal WCP across the range of λ\lambda values considered, while still attaining the target coverage level.

H.2.2 Outcome Noise

Figure 9 studies the effect of the outcome noise level σε\sigma_{\varepsilon}. When the noise level is small, the nonconformity scores are determined primarily by the deterministic exposure mechanism, and changes in peer exposure induced by the target intervention can substantially alter the calibration scores. In this regime, WCP falls below the nominal coverage level, especially in the transductive setting.

As σε\sigma_{\varepsilon} increases, the contribution of noise to the variability of the nonconformity scores grows. In this regime, WCP becomes closer to ideal WCP, and its empirical coverage degradation is reduced. IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ maintain coverage above the target level in both the transductive and inductive settings across the range of noise levels considered. Larger noise levels naturally lead to wider prediction sets for all methods, and the gap between IA-WCP and other baselines is most visible in the large-noise regime.

H.2.3 Interference Locality

Figure 10 varies the number of groups GG, which controls the locality of interference. For fixed NN, smaller values of GG correspond to larger peer groups. In this regime, changing the treatment of a target unit, or embedding a new treated unit in the inductive setting, can affect a larger fraction of the calibration sample. The discrepancy between the observational and interventional calibration scores is therefore larger for smaller values of GG.

For small values of GG, WCP coverage falls below the nominal level. As GG increases, peer groups become smaller and interference becomes more localized. As a result, the observational calibration scores used by WCP become closer to the ideal interventional scores, and the empirical coverage of WCP improves, approaching that of ideal WCP. IA-WCP and IA-WCP+ compensate for the presence of interference, and their coverage levels remain above the nominal level throughout. As GG grows, the correction term in IA-WCP becomes smaller, so the conservativeness of the method decreases and its performance approaches that of ideal WCP.

H.2.4 Base Predictors

We conclude by evaluating the performance of WCP, ideal WCP, IA-WCP, and IA-WCP+ with the different base predictors introduced in Section 4.2.

Figure 11 reports the empirical coverage and normalized width of the prediction sets obtained using these methods and predictors. As expected, the mismatched interference-free predictor yields the widest prediction sets, whereas the predictor fitted using both XX and EE is the most efficient. We also observe that the miscoverage gap of WCP is larger when using the interference-free predictor. In contrast, with the fitted predictors, the coverage achieved by WCP is much closer to the target level, despite the absence of coverage guarantees. The proposed methods, IA-WCP and IA-WCP+, remain valid for all predictors considered, and their efficiency increases with the quality of the base predictor.
